title: Village Between Two Armies
disclaimer: FICTIONAL RECONSTRUCTION. This scenario is created for educational purposes and is based on documented historical conditions. You are playing a fictional character — it does not represent the exact life of a specific historical individual.

intro.youAre: You are the head of a farming household in a village in the Gangetic plain, north of Delhi. For years your family has planted, harvested, paid land revenue, and borrowed from the moneylender when the rains failed.
intro.where: A village in the Gangetic plain, north of Delhi
intro.context: In the spring of 1857 there was unrest among the soldiers of the East India Company's Bengal Army. By the second week of May, that unrest has spilled onto the roads. Armies — Company and rebel — will both need food, fodder and labour. Villages like yours sit in their way.

narrative: Your life has always moved to the weight of two clocks: the monsoon and the revenue collector. Both are now uncertain.
News from the world arrives slowly, and it arrives as rumour.
Every person who passes your gate — a sepoy, a trader, a beggar — carries a different story.

stages.title: Rumours at the Well
stages.description: You hear news at the well that soldiers at Meerut — a day's march away — have risen against their officers and marched to Delhi. Some neighbours say the Company is finished. Others say the soldiers were criminals. One old man insists: 'The cartridge, they say, greased with pig and cow fat. That is what they are fighting about.' The air changes. No one knows what comes next.

choices.label: Remain in your village
choices.summary: Hold the household together and wait for clearer news.
choices.consequence: The village binds tighter. Crops still need tending, and you begin quietly storing grain. But the village is isolated — no trader comes, and the only news is rumour. For a week you know nothing of the war.
choices.historicalContext: Most people in the Gangetic countryside in 1857 did not choose sides in a battle. They chose how to keep a household going while soldiers and revenue officials moved around them. Isolation made rumour stronger than fact.

choices.label: Travel to the nearby market
choices.summary: Walk to the market town for news and supplies.
choices.consequence: You reach the market two days later. It is changed — half the stalls shut, prices climbing, soldiers' parties riding through. You learn that Delhi is in rebel hands and the Company is gathering armies. You buy what you can carry, but on the way home you are stopped by a patrol and forced to hand over a load of grain.
choices.historicalContext: Armies requisitioned grain, animals and labour as they moved. Holding a village's stores drew their attention; hiding them risked their anger. Traders and cultivators alike learned to read the road before using it.

choices.label: Seek information from local contacts
choices.summary: Ask kin, the headman, and passing travellers what they truly know.
choices.consequence: Your contacts paint a fuller picture: the sepoys hold Delhi and the old emperor has been pushed into leading them; Company columns are marching from the south. Your oldest uncle argues the family should store grain and hide the best bullocks. You agree — but word of your meeting spreads, and you are now 'a man who knows things'.
choices.historicalContext: In an era without newspapers reaching every village, kin networks, pilgrims, sepoy letters and caravan gossip were the news media of 1857. Historians study exactly these networks to trace how the rebellion spread.

stages.title: The Demand Comes
stages.description: Two riders stop at the headman's door. They say they come in the name of the rebellion: the emperor has declared that villages should support the rising — grain for soldiers, and men if called. A magistrate, they add, would come soon. That night a neighbour flees to his wife's village across the river.

choices.label: Hide part of your grain reserve
choices.summary: Conceal grain in a false floor under the cattle shed.
choices.consequence: You bury wheat in an oiled cloth beneath the straw. It is heavy, secret work. Weeks later, soldiers searching for supplies find the shed — and enough of it — but not the false floor. You eat through the autumn on it. The risk is that discovery meant ruin, or worse.
choices.historicalContext: Hoarding, hiding grain and false floors are documented responses of villages to armies on the march in 1857. Requisitioning was a fact of life — the question was always who you hid it from.

choices.label: Offer grain and support to the uprising
choices.summary: Contribute openly to the riders' cause.
choices.consequence: You give a bullock-load of grain and a promise. The riders mark the village as friendly, and for a season you are left in peace by rebel bands. But an informer repeats your name to a Company officer across the river, and you begin sleeping under the roof of the granary.
choices.historicalContext: Support for the rebellion was not uniform. Villages, castes, landlords and faiths split in complicated ways. Supporting one side made you a target of the other — a lesson every landlord in the Doab learned in 1857.

choices.label: Send a family member to learn the truth
choices.summary: Dispatch your brother to Delhi to see what the emperor's rule means.
choices.consequence: Your brother returns after two weeks with a sober report: Delhi is in chaos, prices hurt, and the emperor's authority reaches only as far as soldiers with guns. He watched a sepoy column requisition whole cartloads. 'Do not believe the posters,' he said. 'Believe your wheat.'
choices.historicalContext: The proclamations issued in Bahadur Shah Zafar's name promised protection of religion and property, and appealed to peasants and landlords. How far those words travelled — and were believed — varied enormously across the countryside.

stages.title: Men With Guns
stages.description: A column of sepoys — deserters heading for Delhi, their faces painted with the signs of a hard march — reaches your village. Their officer demands a meal for his men and fodder for the horses. Behind him, the village's women have already begun hiding the young men in the fields.

choices.label: Feed the soldiers and send them on
choices.summary: Provide a meal and fodder, and ask only for safe passage.
choices.consequence: You cook for the column. They leave at dusk, unharmed, and the village is spared a search. But the headman, afraid of the Company's revenge, later denounces you to no one in particular — and the cost of the feast is a month of your stores.
choices.historicalContext: Hospitality under coercion was survival, not loyalty. Hundreds of thousands of non-combatants fed marching armies in 1857 because refusal was often the only alternative to destruction.

choices.label: Hide your stores and refuse
choices.summary: Pretend the village is empty and hope they pass.
choices.consequence: The ruse holds for an hour, then a search finds the cattle. They take the two best pairs of bullocks and burn the headman's cart-house. No one is killed — but the village is afraid now in a way it was not before.
choices.historicalContext: Cattle, bullocks and carts were among the most valued resources of the 1857 countryside, conscripted by both sides. Their loss crippled a household's ploughing for a season.

choices.label: Take the family and flee toward relatives
choices.summary: Leave the village at night for a relative's holding near the river.
choices.consequence: You walk eleven kilometres through the dark. The relative takes you in — grudgingly, for mouths to feed — and you spend a month watching the road. When you return, the roof is intact but the winter crop is ruined. Safety, at the price of the year.
choices.historicalContext: Flight was a common response. Accounts of 1857 record villages emptied by fear, and families moving between kin. The displaced carried memory — and sometimes the news — with them.

stages.title: The Season Turns
stages.description: The rains approach and the fields must be planted for the winter food supply. But no one is certain who will rule by harvest time. Elder farmers argue: 'Plant for our own mouths,' they say. 'Whatever comes, the land must be sown.' And at the edge of the discussion sits the never-solved question: who will collect the revenue, and with what right?

choices.label: Sow for the next season whatever happens
choices.summary: Plant the fields, borrow seed, and bet on the land itself.
choices.consequence: You plant early, before most others, and the rains bless the seed. By harvest, the land is the only thing that did not change sides. Your family eats. In a year of war, that is a small victory.
choices.historicalContext: Peasants kept planting through the war — the harvest was the real debate about sovereignty. Whoever collected it, the field produced. The resilience of cultivation is why the Gangetic economy recovered within a few seasons.

choices.label: Seek a written assurance from the district
choices.summary: Ask whichever authority holds the district to promise revenue terms in writing.
choices.consequence: You walk to the district town and present yourself. The officer on duty scribbles a signed slip promising to 'fix the revenue for the current year' — a scrap of paper worth less than its ink once the front moves. But you now know how the district is governed, and that knowledge keeps you out of debt.
choices.historicalContext: Revenue responsibility was the pivot of 1857 politics. The Company's governments fought land questions as fiercely as armies fought battles. Written promises, sighted in advance, shaped who felt safe to cooperate.

choices.label: Leave part of the family with kin near a large town
choices.summary: Split the household — some to the relative, some to guard the fields.
choices.consequence: Splitting the family halves the risk and doubles the worry. Your brother's family stays at the tank village; you guard the fields. Through the autumn you receive letters carried by traders — the only post that still runs.
choices.historicalContext: Family dispersal was a buffer against loss in 1857 villages. Households that could send members to kin in another district survived shocks better than those that could not.

stages.title: After the Storm
stages.description: The front has rolled past. Delhi has fallen back to Company columns; the roads are policed again, and the revenue settlement is being re-imposed. Neighbours drift back from hiding. The moneylender has reopened his ledger. The world wants its accounts settled — including yours.

choices.label: Return, cooperate, and settle your dues
choices.summary: Present yourself, pay what is owed, and rebuild on the books.
choices.consequence: You deal with the collector, settle the arrears with the moneylender, and go back to work. It is not a happy ending — it is a practical one. The village is whole, poorer, and strangely numb. There are no stories of heroes here, only of surviving.
choices.historicalContext: By late 1858, Company order was restored across most of northern India, and revenue demands rose again. The cost of the upheaval — lives, grain and cattle — was largely borne, as always, by the cultivators.

choices.label: Return slowly, half the family first
choices.summary: Test the peace before committing the whole household.
choices.consequence: Your brother returns first and reports the roads safe. You follow a fortnight later. The delay costs you a season's crop share but saves you from the worst of the first wave of requisitions. Cautious, a little older, you rebuild more slowly than your neighbours.
choices.historicalContext: Rebuilding was uneven. Some villages recovered within a year; others lost plough cattle or titles and fell into debt that lasted generations. The aftermath, like the war, was experienced village by village.

choices.label: Stay low and keep your distance from officials
choices.summary: Never fully return; work quietly and avoid the collector's eye.
choices.consequence: You farm cautiously, pay little, and are marked by the village as 'the one who stayed hidden.' A year later a dispute over cattle drags you before the collector's court — where your absence comes back to count against you. The land kept you alive; the law now half-owns your time.
choices.historicalContext: Distance from authority preserved lives in 1857 but entangled households in later disputes. The courts of the re-established state remembered who had absented themselves, and land titles turned on it.

ending.title: Your Village, One Year Later
ending.text: The war of 1857 passed across your life the way a flood passes across a field — it changed the lines of everything without making a sound. You did not fire a gun. You fed men who had guns. You hid wheat, counted cattle, and watched the roads. In the ledger of the rebellion, your name appears nowhere. But the rebellion happened, in part, among people exactly like you.
lessons: Most people in the region in 1857 never fought a battle — they lived through the war.
Armies needed grain, cattle and labour, and villages paid all three.
Land revenue and debt shaped rural life long before any cartridge.
Rumour was the news media of the countryside; facts arrived late and on foot.

title: The Oath and the Cartridge
disclaimer: FICTIONAL RECONSTRUCTION. This scenario is created for educational purposes and is based on documented historical conditions. You are playing a fictional character — it does not represent the exact life of a specific historical individual.

intro.youAre: You are a sepoy in a regiment of the East India Company's Bengal Army — a professional soldier who has sworn to the Company, draws pay, and carries a decorated musket. You have served campaigns and citations.
intro.where: A cantonment of the Bengal Army in north India
intro.context: In your regiment there is talk — and now near-certainty — that the new Enfield cartridges are greased with animal fat that would defile both Hindu and Muslim soldiers who must bite them open. Officers say it is nonsense. Comrades say the Company has ceased to care.

narrative: You joined the colours when the Company was a known thing — orderly, regular, generous to its soldiers.
Now the order is to load the new cartridge, and every man in the line is thinking of the same things: his oath, his mother, his gods.
There is a rumour that the whole army is to be disarmed, and a letter from home that says the villages are already empty of young men.

stages.title: The Cartridges Arrive
stages.description: The stores issue the new Enfield cartridges and a drill is announced. By the evening, the bazaar has finished the rumour: the grease is beef and pork fat. Men gather in the evening, low-voiced, outside the lamp posts. 'They wish to break our caste and our faith together,' says an elder havildar. The officers' reassurance sounds, to the ranks, thin.

choices.label: Refuse the cartridge openly
choices.summary: Decline on the parade ground and face the consequence.
choices.consequence: You refuse, and others follow. The commanding officer's patience breaks; you are placed under arrest, tried by court-martial and sentenced to years of hard labour in irons — the exact punishment you had watched troopers receive at Meerut a week earlier. In irons, you are marched past your own regiment.
choices.historicalContext: The refusal at Meerut was not an isolated event — refusals and courts-martial marked the spring of 1857 across Bengal Army stations. The public spectacle of punishment embittered garrisons far beyond the men sentenced.

choices.label: Obey, but speak only to your friends
choices.summary: Do the drill and keep your doubts private.
choices.consequence: You drill with the cartridge and feel the weight of your comrades' changed eyes. That night your closest friend tells you plainly: 'They are making dogs of us.' Obedience has cost you no punishment — but it has cost you standing among the men you must stand beside.
choices.historicalContext: Many sepoys complied under pressure while privately sharing grievances. The army was not united in refusal in early 1857 — it divided man from man, company from company.

choices.label: Seek reassurance from your officers
choices.summary: Ask directly, man to man, what the grease really is.
choices.consequence: Your officer swears the fat is not animal — or swears he does not know. His discomfort tells you all you need. He is a decent man who does not know more than you do. The cartridge sits in its box between you. Neither of you has answered the question.
choices.historicalContext: Officer-sepoy trust disintegrated in 1857 along exactly this fault line: the Company's officers could not confirm what was in the cartridges, so every reassurance sounded like a lie — documented repeatedly in court-martial testimony. There was no grease the Company could prove clean.

stages.title: The Example
stages.description: Word reaches the barracks that at Meerut, eighty-five troopers of the cavalry refused the cartridge, were court-martialled, and have been stripped, chained and marched to prison in front of the whole cantonment — those same men being the pride of the garrison. Your regiment is ordered to prepare for a similar drill. The night, in the bazaars, is loud with talk of Delhi and the emperor.

choices.label: Prepare to rise with your comrades
choices.summary: Join the shared plan quietly forming around the lamps.
choices.consequence: You are part of the plan — which most of the garrison's Indian soldiers know by nightfall. Sunday brings a sudden order: the Europeans draw arms. The plan becomes action, and you move with your regiment toward the gates, fired on from the way of the church, in the smoke and noise of a cantonment coming apart.
choices.historicalContext: The Meerut rising of 10 May 1857 was precisely such a plan-without-a-date that the army's orders ignited at a fixed hour. Soldiers chose — or were swept — into the same action across scores of garrisons in the following weeks.

choices.label: Hold back and watch which way the wind turns
choices.summary: Stand with your own and burn no bridges — yet.
choices.consequence: You stand guard through the night while the cantonment tears itself open. Morning finds the European camp burning and the sepoys moving off. Your restraint lets you and your section serve as messengers — but it also marks you, later, as a man the rebels could not quite trust, and the Company could not quite believe.
choices.historicalContext: Scores of sepoys and units tried to stay neutral in May 1857 — standing aside from an uprising without joining it. In the chaos such neutrality was almost impossible, and few maintained it for long.

choices.label: Warn the officers of what you have heard
choices.summary: Try to hold the regiment to its colours.
choices.consequence: You pass word to a junior officer, who credits you and files a report. The officers disbelieve it, or cannot act; the report is buried. You have fed the machine's own rumour. When the rising comes — as the report said it would — no one remembers your warning, only that you were seen speaking with the officers.
choices.historicalContext: Some soldiers did warn officers of the coming storm, and their warnings were recorded in Company archives — the disbelieving officers noted as often as the informants. Loyalty was neither simple nor safe.

stages.title: The Road to Delhi
stages.description: The regiment is marching — toward Delhi, toward the Red Fort, toward the old emperor who has been forced to chair a war. On the road, villagers bring food, and old men place marks of blessing on the soldiers. Ahead of you, you are told, is a war to free the faith; behind you is the oath you swore. Both are loud in your head at different hours.

choices.label: March on with the rebels to Delhi
choices.summary: Carry the colours toward the Red Fort.
choices.consequence: You enter Delhi in mid-May amid massed regiments, drums and the emperor's uncertain blessing. For a season you are part of something: city, army, cause. Then the British columns begin their siege, and Delhi's defence eats its own soldiers — hunger, fever and desertion among the thin honours.
choices.historicalContext: Thousands of sepoys marched to Delhi in May 1857 and fought in its defence until September, when the columns stormed the city. Delhi's defence and fall is documented in extensive British and local accounts — including sepoys deserting as the siege tightened.

choices.label: Slip away to the villages
choices.summary: Leave the road and disappear into the countryside.
choices.consequence: You melt away at a ford before the revolt's second week, walking all night to reach your home village. Months pass in hiding — fed by kin, watched by informers. The Company's searches for 'mutinous sowars' pass within sight of your door more than once. You survive the war; the war does not end for you for another year.
choices.historicalContext: Desertion dissolved armies on both sides. Thousands of Indian soldiers slipped away from the rebellion's armies, and the Company's own ranks thinned as hastily recruited men crossed the lines to their villages.

choices.label: Remain with the Company's colours
choices.summary: Turn your section back toward regimental authority.
choices.consequence: You rejoin the Company's forces as the rebellion consolidates. Your section is used as scouts — trusted men who know the countryside. You serve through the reconquest of Delhi, twisting in your saddle each time the enemy is 'your own people.' The Company pays your back-arrears and never fully trusts you again.
choices.historicalContext: Loyal regiments — Sikh, Punjabi, Gurkha and steadier Indian units — were the backbone of the British reconquest. Some Indian soldiers chose the Company's side and fought against the rising, a fact basic to understanding 1857.

stages.title: The Siege Tightens
stages.description: Whichever road you chose, it is late autumn. Delhi is under artillery fire or fallen; the Company reconquers town by town. The last armies of the rising are disintegrating, and men who a season ago were soldiers are now fugitives — or garrisons. In the cold morning, the roads carry both armies, and the dust remembers everything.

choices.label: Stay to the end, whatever the end is
choices.summary: Hold your post through the last stand.
choices.consequence: You are among the last to hold, fighting through the final weeks until the lines break. Captured, you are marched with other sepoy prisoners to the tryals and the common jails. The Company calls you rebel; your comrades call you faithful. You will spend years in prison and answer for a war you never chose.
choices.historicalContext: Thousands of rebel soldiers were captured, tried or simply dispersed in 1858. Wide amnesties were later declared in the Queen's Proclamation. The war's end was not clean: it left prisoners, dacoits and famished villages behind it.

choices.label: Slip away to your home by night
choices.summary: Leave the colours and the cause both.
choices.consequence: You return to your village in the last weeks of the war, a deserter twice over. The village knows better than to ask. You sleep a year under a false name, ploughing, until the amnesty makes it safe to live as yourself again. The Company's records show one more 'missing' sowar; the village records show a man who came home.
choices.historicalContext: The Queen's Proclamation of November 1858 offered amnesty and pardon to most rebels who had not murdered British prisoners. Vast numbers of deserters returned to villages under that promise, and the Proclamation's careful wording was read, and relied on, at village level.

choices.label: Surrender and take the amnesty
choices.summary: Give yourself up under the declared terms.
choices.consequence: You surrender under the proclamation's terms, hand in your arms, and receive the newly issued pardon. The army has been reorganised: new regiments, new pay rules, and darker suspicions where the old names are read aloud. You are discharged, not welcomed. The war ends for you with a signature on a form.
choices.historicalContext: After 1858 the British restructured the army, doubling European ratios and changing recruiting practices. Indian soldiers fought for the Crown again within a generation — in a force consciously 'reorganised' in 1857's shadow.

ending.title: The Colours and the Cartridge
ending.text: You carried the oath and the cartridge together for as long as any soldier could. In the end, the war of 1857 broke the Bengal Army into pieces — some of its soldiers became its conquerors, some its fugitives, and the army itself was rebuilt so it could never hold such a grip on its own country again. What remains, in the old muster books, are names — and behind each one a man who stood at the exact place where an empire's trust failed.
lessons: The Bengal Army's soldiers outnumbered its British officers and soldiers many times over.
Oath, religion, family and pay pulled the same men in opposing directions.
The rebellion did not happen everywhere at once, and not every soldier joined it.
After 1858 the British rebuilt the army with different recruiting and control.

title: The Loom and the Fire
tagline: June 1857 — a weaver's quarter in a town of the Doab
disclaimer: FICTIONAL RECONSTRUCTION. This scenario is created for educational purposes and is based on documented historical conditions. You are playing a fictional character — it does not represent the exact life of a specific historical individual.

intro.youAre: You are a weaver in a cloth-manufacturing quarter of a town on the Ganga-Yamuna doab. Your family has worked the loom for generations, selling to traders who carried the cloth down the trunk roads. In recent years those traders have paid less; cheaper factory-spun yarn and imported goods have narrowed the craft.
intro.where: A cloth-manufacturing quarter of a town in the Doab
intro.context: The rising has reached your town. The old shopfronts are shut; courts and treasuries have changed hands. Orders are cancelled overnight, and every armed group that passes wants cloth, thread or money. The craft that fed you has become, overnight, a thing to be defended or lost.

narrative: The loom runs, but the market has vanished.
In the quarter, talk is of two things only: what has happened to the town, and what will happen to the weavers.
Somewhere in this conflict, someone will still want cloth — the question is who, and how they pay.

stages.title: The Order is Cancelled
stages.description: A trader cancels a year's standing order the morning after the treasury changes hands. Your stock — fine cloth, yarn, dyes — sits in the loft. Your neighbour, a darzi with a busy shop, tells you soldiers are buying cloth for turbans and uniforms on the other side of the town. Two of the quarter's weavers are already hired by the armed party holding the gate.

choices.label: Seek out the new buyers
choices.summary: Take cloth samples to the armed party holding the gate.
choices.consequence: You find the officer of the party and sell a roll of cloth at a good price — paid in coin that is worth less, it turns out, than it is (the treasury was emptied). The party promises further orders. For a season the loom runs steady. But your name is now on a list that a clerk will remember later.
choices.historicalContext: Armies in 1857 were immediate customers for cloth — turbans, uniforms, flags and tents. Artisans dealt with whoever held the town. Post-war inquiries into 'collaboration' worked from ledgers exactly like the one you entered your name into.

choices.label: Lay low and conserve your thread
choices.summary: Stop the looms and guard what stock you have.
choices.consequence: The looms fall silent for six weeks. You live on savings and hope. When the town's trade slowly resumes, your stock is intact but your customers have scattered — the traders you trusted once have not returned. You survive, but your craft has stepped off its rhythm.
choices.historicalContext: Many artisans chose hoarding and caution over alliance. The craft quarters of towns like Kanpur, Lucknow and Delhi were hit hard by months of siege, blockade and requisition — work stopped whether or not its owner chose a side.

choices.label: Join the artisans gathering at the bazaar
choices.summary: Mingle where the craft and the crowd meet.
choices.consequence: The bazaar's artisans, dispossessed and angry, draft a letter supporting the rising in the emperor's name — and your name is added. It is a crowd act, half-coerced, half-heartfelt. Months later the letter resurfaces in an inquiry into 'leading persons of the quarter' and costs you a season under suspicion.
choices.historicalContext: The proclamations of 1857 made direct appeals to artisans, weavers and the urban poor, promising protection of religion and livelihood. Whether such appeals worked, or were merely read out in courtyards, is a live historical question.

stages.title: The Search
stages.description: Three days later, a squad of soldiers — this time from the Company's side — enters your quarter claiming deserters are being harboured. They pull bolt, loom and copper to the floor looking under the platform of the house. The roll of fine cloth you set aside for the festival is taken for 'requisition'. They leave a printed chit promising payment 'when order is restored.'

choices.label: Take the chit and sell to them willingly
choices.summary: Trade with the Company's commissariat on paper terms.
choices.consequence: You present the chit at the commissariat and are paid — in paper that the collectors later refuse at face value. But the supply officer remembers your work and keeps your loom busy through the end of the war, supplying cloth to the garrison at fixed prices. You are professional again; you are also, to your quarter, 'the one who works for the Company.'
choices.historicalContext: The Company's wartime administration lived on such paper promises — receipts and chits that changed value when the front moved. Artisan workshops contracted to armies made real money and real enemies simultaneously.

choices.label: Hide your best loom and thread
choices.summary: Dismantle the equipment into hiding and work on a spare.
choices.consequence: The best loom goes up into the roof space, disassembled, piece by piece through a false panel. You work on an old frame for the rest of the season, producing half the output. When peace returns, the hidden loom is worth more than everything else you own — and nothing has been lost but a season.
choices.historicalContext: Hiding productive equipment — looms, anvils, presses — was a documented response of craftsmen to requisitioning. Equipment was both capital and memory; hiding it was the artisan's version of hoarding grain.

choices.label: Leave the quarter for another town
choices.summary: Pack what you can and follow traders' roads east.
choices.consequence: You close the house and walk with your family toward a town on the lower doab, carrying your yarn and your best shuttle. The town has not fallen into the war. You find work, poorer-paying, in another loom shed and sleep on the floor of a relative's courtyard. The quarter you left is still there when you return, months later, thinner.
choices.historicalContext: Artisan mobility was shaped by the routes of trade and the reach of war. Towns off the main routes sheltered craftsmen through 1857; the cost was lower wages and harder living.

stages.title: After the Fire
stages.description: Months pass. The town changes hands once more and order is re-imposed under the Crown's new government. The quarter survives — quieter, with fewer hands. Traders return for cloth. Some weavers reopen their shops; others, the strongest, have been carried away into the army's workshops or into service. The old order of custom and credit has been rewritten in ink, and your craft must learn the new lines.

choices.label: Rebuild the workshop and trade again
choices.summary: Reopen, find traders, and let the loom speak.
choices.consequence: You rebuild modestly, selling to the same kinds of traders under the new administration. The market is slower and cheaper; factory yarn eats at the edges. But the loom turns, the family eats, and your name is in the 'new lists' of the quarter — a small purchase back into citizenship.
choices.historicalContext: In the years after 1858 the towns recovered gradually, but textile crafts faced a long squeeze as industrial imports widened. The weavers' resilience was of a kind economists now chart in official trade returns.

choices.label: Shift to work the new demand
choices.summary: Adjust your craft toward what the new economy buys.
choices.consequence: You put down your fine looms and take up the coarser, faster work the new officials and markets want — rough cloth, cords, canvas. It is less beautiful work and more secure pay. The old dances of the festival cloth are a memory; the household is fed. You look at the fine loom on the wall like a picture of a previous life.
choices.historicalContext: Colonial and post-1857 demand shifted from fine handwork to coarse mass cloth. Craftsmen adapted toward the coarser goods; fine craft quarter declined. The economic reordering was as consequential as the war itself.

choices.label: Hold to the fine craft and its honour
choices.summary: Refuse the coarse shift and keep the old technique.
choices.consequence: You keep the fine looms and turn the few festival and court commissions that survive. It costs you years of leanness and the respect of the practical traders, who say you 'hold to the old ways.' But a museum, one day, will call what you preserved a craft — and a younger weaver, one day, will ask you how the pattern was made.
choices.historicalContext: Fine craft did not vanish at once; it survived in diminished channels — courts, ritual, wealth. Its preservation preserved techniques that industrial weaving later could not replace. That is why the craft continues to matter today.

ending.title: Loom and Ledger
ending.text: In 1857 the biggest part of your war was not a battle — it was keeping the loom turning, the thread dry, and the family fed while the world's ledgers were being rewritten around you. The rising, the reconquest, the Proclamation: they passed like weather across your quarter. What your hands held — the thread, the pattern, the craft — was small against empires. But it was what the empires fought over, and it is what survived them.
lessons: The industrial and colonial economy had been squeezing crafts long before the war began.
Artisans supplied both sides — turbans, uniforms, tents — and were paid in promises that changed value.
Craft equipment was capital: artisans hid looms as carefully as farmers hid grain.
After 1858 the towns recovered, but the fine trades slowly yielded to coarser industrial markets.

title: The Ledger of Uncertain Roads
tagline: June 1857 — a merchant's house, north India
disclaimer: FICTIONAL RECONSTRUCTION. This scenario is created for educational purposes and is based on documented historical conditions. You are playing a fictional character — it does not represent the exact life of a specific historical individual.

intro.youAre: You are a merchant with a house in one of the bazaar towns of the doab. Your family's ledger runs across four towns — credit advanced to weavers and farmers, grain and cloth moved down the trunk roads, bullion and coin counted in the inner room.
intro.where: A bazaar town of the Ganga-Yamuna doab
intro.context: The rising has cut the roads. Debt spread through four towns now cannot be collected; stock sits in warehouses on both sides of a front line that moves without announcement. In such times, credit is a rumour — and rumour is the only credit that works.

narrative: Your family has always said the true wealth of a merchant is a road he can trust.
Now the road is an argument between armies.
Every choice you make tonight is a line someone will read in the ledger tomorrow.

stages.title: The Warehouses
stages.description: Word comes that a warehouse you own has been requisitioned by soldiers holding the river crossing — grain and coarse cloth taken against a signed chit. The other warehouse, across the river, is under the Company's hand. Your cousin writes from that side: 'They are taking everything from the bazaar for the army. Come and help us, or the shop will be empty.'

choices.label: Move what you can under cover of night
choices.summary: Quietly shift the best stock to hidden godowns.
choices.consequence: Under lantern-light you move the best bolts and bullion to a potting house no one associates with you, paying moving men handsomely. The ruse holds; when the soldiers return for the remainder, they find a warehouse already emptied by their own side's fire. What you saved is worth what it always was — but the courage it took is not in any ledger.
choices.historicalContext: Merchants across the doab hid stock, moved bullion and used false ledgers in 1857. Company quartermasters and rebel collectors both lived on requisition; the merchant's craft was to keep half a step ahead of both.

choices.label: Play both sides with written promises
choices.summary: Sell promises to each authority, collect from whomever lasts.
choices.consequence: You deal with both camps through clerks, keeping a clean ledger for each. For a while it works — cargo moves once, then twice; both sides sign. Then the two ledgers collide in a single office, and you are brought in for fraud by the very authority you tried to satisfy. Your family's name, bought at such cost, buys you a release at a heavy fine.
choices.historicalContext: Deliberate double-dealing was common and dangerous. Post-war courts-martial and commissions examined merchants' papers for precisely this pattern of 'selling to both sides' — a trade that could end in confiscation.

choices.label: Hold steady and wait for order
choices.summary: Keep the house shut and let the storm pass.
choices.consequence: You refuse to move stock or deal. For three months your warehouses sit untouched — partly luck, partly because both armies had better targets. When trade slowly resumes, you are the rare merchant who loses nothing and gains the trust of the new administration, which pays promptly for the stock it needs. It is a lesson your grandson will repeat: 'In riot, the safest ledger is a shut one.'
choices.historicalContext: Neutrality was a business strategy. Merchants who kept their books shut and houses bolted weathered the war better than those who chose sides — though in some towns neutrality itself was taken for alliance.

stages.title: The Road Again Opens
stages.description: After weeks of closure, a road is reopened under a guard of armed traders. Prices at the capital are said to be double. A partner urges you to send a caravan of the grain you hold to market while the price holds. The risks: bandits, soldiers, confiscation. The reward: a season's profit in one journey.

choices.label: Send the caravan while prices hold
choices.summary: Move the grain to market under armed guard.
choices.consequence: The caravan runs — and is held at three checkpoints for 'duties' that consume a fifth of its value. Still, you sell at the doubled price and return with more silver than you left with. On the third journey a soldier detaches the guard and takes the rest of the stock as 'requisition.' The profit of two journeys is lost in the third. Net result: a narrow escape and a stubborn lesson.
choices.historicalContext: Contested roads carried miraculously high prices and brutal tolls. Both armies taxed movement through fines, 'duties' and outright seizure — the cost of moving goods in 1857 climbed several-fold over peacetime.

choices.label: Sit on the grain and await real news
choices.summary: Hold the stock until the front draws a clear line.
choices.consequence: You hold while partners sell — and their profit is real, while your caution looks like cowardice. Then the front shifts: the market that was hungry is now over-supplied by captured stores, and the price collapses. You won your argument and lost your money. In the ledger of the house, caution is entered as its own cost.
choices.historicalContext: Price gyrated wildly with every shift of the front as grain markets swung between famine and glut. Those who timed by news agents did better than those who timed by feeling — merchants' correspondence survives to tell us so.

choices.label: Lend the grain to the army on contract
choices.summary: Sell bulk to whichever commissariat holds the town, on paper.
choices.consequence: You contract the whole store to the commissariat at a fixed price — lower than the market, but certain, and in signed agreement. The agreement is honoured. When the market collapses weeks later, yours is the one house in the quarter that is paid, uninterrupted. The traders call you cautious; you call yourself covered.
choices.historicalContext: Army contracts sustained many merchant houses through 1857. The commissariat's need for grain was constant, and contracts were among the few paper promises both sides kept — because they kept needed supplies coming.

stages.title: The End of the Year
stages.description: A year has passed. The war is over in the doab, and the Crown's new government rules the roads. Your partners want to rebuild the partnership — lend again, open branches, reclaim the old routes. The dust of the conflict has settled long enough that trade is again the talk of the bazaar. But the ledger of the last year must be closed first: who pays, who never pays, and what the house is now worth.

choices.label: Reopen full trade on the old terms
choices.summary: Resume lending, branch-houses and trunk-road caravans.
choices.consequence: You reopen boldly. Within two years the house has reclaimed its place — the roads are safer than they have been in a generation, and the Crown's courts enforce debts more reliably than the old Company's did. You have survived the greatest fire in the family's memory and built on the ashes. Somewhere in the boxes is the receipt of the two ledgers; you keep it to remind yourself what a year of war costs a house of commerce.
choices.historicalContext: In the years after 1858 the trade economy of north India recovered strongly under a more regular Crown administration and a better-enforced revenue and credit system. The merchants who had weathered the war prospered in the peace.

choices.label: Rebuild cautiously, with contracts only
choices.summary: Lend only against hard collateral and written agreements.
choices.consequence: You finance the rebuilding deliberately — every loan secured, every branch watched. It slows the house's growth but buys it safety in the years of settlement disputes that follow the war. When the 'mutiny claims' are processed, yours is among the first and fastest paid, because your papers were always in order.
choices.historicalContext: After 1858, courts and colonial administration pushed commerce toward written contracts and registered debts. The merchant houses that adapted early to formal credit made the transition smoothest.

choices.label: Spread capital into new ventures
choices.summary: Buy land, finance reform-era enterprise, open an agency.
choices.consequence: You diversify out of pure trade — buying village land, financing a printing venture, opening an agency that handles the new paperwork of the Crown's government. It is the decision of a house, not a merchant: your capital changes form, and with it the family. When the old bazaar traders speak of you, they say you have become 'a man of the new century' before the century has begun.
choices.historicalContext: The post-1858 economy rewarded those who diversified into land, services and the professions that a growing colonial state required. Some merchant capital made exactly this long turn toward the modern.

ending.title: The Distance Between Two Ledgers
ending.text: In 1857 your true assets were never counted in grains and bolts. They were counted in roads you could trust, promises that could be redeemed, and clerks who could be believed when the front moved without warning. The war closed your ledgers for a season — and opened them again on new terms. Whatever you lost to checkpoints and requisitions, you kept the one thing that mattered: a house that could still trade when the firing stopped.
lessons: Credit extended across four towns could not be collected when the roads closed — merchants lived or died by debt.
Both armies taxed movement through duties and requisition, and prices swung wildly with every shift of the front.
Army contracts paid well and regularly, but made a merchant a target of the other side.
After 1858 the Crown's courts and contracts rebuilt trade more durably than war had broken it.

title: Schoolroom Under Siege
tagline: June 1857 — a city of letters in crisis
disclaimer: FICTIONAL RECONSTRUCTION. This scenario is created for educational purposes and is based on documented historical conditions. You are playing a fictional character — it does not represent the exact life of a specific historical individual.

intro.youAre: You are a young person of a literate family in a north Indian city — Delhi, or one of the provincial capitals. Your learning mixes the old world (Persian and Urdu, the classics, the madrasa or pathshala) with the new (an English school, print, the new sciences).
intro.where: A city of learning in northern India
intro.context: The rising has reached your city. Schools have shut; teachers have scattered; the printing district is full of proclamations and the city's libraries are guarded and watched. Everyone with a pen or a printing press is suddenly important to both sides — and nobody studies in a siege.

narrative: Your education was meant to make you useful to a new century.
The century, so far, is choosing other methods.
But what you carry — languages, letters, the habit of careful reading — is exactly what the conflict now needs of you.

stages.title: The School Closes
stages.description: Your teacher dismisses the class with a single sentence: 'Return when the city is quiet.' On the way home you pass the printing shops, where sheets are being run off — proclamations in Urdu and Persian, orders, denunciations. A poet friend of your uncle's calls you over and asks: 'You can read well. Come and help us check this text against the original. The whole city will read your line tomorrow.'

choices.label: Help with the text at the print shop
choices.summary: Read the proof against the original for the cost of another night.
choices.consequence: You spend the night at the print shop, checking the proclamation against the original — and catch an error that would have miswritten the name of the emperor. The printer thanks you; the sheet goes out correct. A month later, when the city changes hands, someone remembers, with interest, who helped whose papers get printed.
choices.historicalContext: The proclamations of 1857 were genuine, printed documents — texts in Urdu and Persian distributed across the north. Their exact wording was painstakingly controlled by both sides, and printing presses were war resources throughout the conflict.

choices.label: Keep studying alone at home
choices.summary: Read and copy texts while the city burns around you.
choices.consequence: You keep to your books, copying a manuscript the teacher left you, as if study were a discipline that war could not cancel. It is — but it is also a way of not looking out the window. When peace returns, your copy is intact, your reading sharper, and you are one of the few students in the city who can say what they lost before it happened.
choices.historicalContext: Libraries and private manuscripts were protected, buried or destroyed during the conflict. Scholarship paused in cities while their literati kept what they could — whole collections were saved by being hidden, exactly as you hid your books.

choices.label: Wander the city and keep a record
choices.summary: Walk the streets, note what you see, and write it down.
choices.consequence: You keep a careful, dated record of the city through the weeks of siege — who came, who went, what was printed, what was burnt. It is a quiet act of scholarship under fire. Years later, a British official seeking 'an accurate account of the mutiny of the native quarters' will find your notebook and pay well for it. You have written a primary source without knowing it.
choices.historicalContext: We know much of what happened in 1857 cities because literate residents kept records — diaries, letters and manuscript chronicles. The genre is real: Indian accounts of the siege of Delhi exist and are studied beside British ones.

stages.title: The Questionnaire
stages.description: A cavalry officer on the Company's side — litter of papers on his table — has a proposition. The city is under reconstruction, and the new administration wants 'trustworthy young men who write well' to transcribe seized papers: letters, proclamations, usury ledgers. The pay is real, the work is sorting the recent past, and half the bazaar regards it as 'serving the conqueror.'

choices.label: Take the transcription work
choices.summary: Copy the seized papers for the new administration.
choices.consequence: You transcribe cartloads of papers — proclamations, creditors' lists, letters — learning more about the city's last months than anyone else alive. The work is honest and useful, and it gives you a place at the table of the new order. But you record, page after page, the letters of men your own family knows, and you carry that knowledge like a secret.
choices.historicalContext: Seized papers, translated and copied by local clerks, are a core source for the history of 1857 — including the proclamations and sepoy letters studied by historians today. Clerks of that generation shaped what the archive remembers.

choices.label: Decline and keep your distance from both sides
choices.summary: Refuse the work and stay at the margin.
choices.consequence: You turn down the posting politely. It costs you a quarrel with your elders and a season of poverty, but it keeps your hands clean in the street's eyes. Months later, when the administration hunts for 'collaborators' and 'loyalists' alike, your name appears in neither column — a rare and strangely valuable place to stand.
choices.historicalContext: Literate young men were courted by both camps in 1857-58. Refusal to be enrolled, on either side, was a real and discreet choice — and its consequences (poverty, safety) are part of the war's ordinary history.

choices.label: Copy for both administrations
choices.summary: Work for whoever holds the city, and keep a second copy.
choices.consequence: You transcribe for whichever side holds the city — and keep a private second copy of everything. The copies become the most valuable thing you own: a full archive of the city's wartime paper. When the files are finally closed, your collection is a record no government possesses. You call it research; your family calls it dangerous.
choices.historicalContext: Private collectors and manuscript copyists are the reason some 1857 documents survive at all. Both official archives and private hoards preserve the paper trail — each transcription another leak in the censors' net.

stages.title: After the Exam
stages.description: Two years later, the city has regained its rhythm. The English school reopens under the Crown's education department; a new course in 'vernacular and native languages' is being formed. Your old teacher urges you to take it and 'become a bridge.' The print shops have resumed, the libraries are patched, and the city is full of young men who must decide what the word 'education' now means.

choices.label: Take the new course in the Crown's school
choices.summary: Learn the new system and become a bridge between worlds.
choices.consequence: You join the new course, learn the new curriculum, and in time become a teacher — a copier of the new order's books. The bridge you build carries government work and government ideas into the old city. In your diary you write that you have done what the war asked: survived, and learned a new grammar.
choices.historicalContext: After 1858 education was reorganised and expanded by the Crown, with 'vernacular' and English tracks dividing the school system. The generation educated in its shadow carried that division into the next century.

choices.label: Return to the older world of learning
choices.summary: Study the classics under private teachers, as the court does.
choices.consequence: You return to Persian and Urdu scholarship under an old master, part of the re-formed world of letters that has survived the war. In a generation this world will seem antique; your learning will be called 'traditional.' You know it as the same craft your grandfather defended — books against the wreckage of the world.
choices.historicalContext: The older literate world — madrasas, pathshalas, Persian and Urdu letters — was neither destroyed nor static; it reconstituted itself in the post-1857 era even as the colonial school system rose beside it.

choices.label: Open a small press of your own
choices.summary: Use the craft of letters to start a business in print.
choices.consequence: You gather a press, type and ink, and begin printing — schoolbooks, a newspaper, pamphlets. It is a poor man's empire, but it is the empire of news, and it grows. Your first publication is the letter you kept from the siege; your last, decades on, is the city's longest-running vernacular paper. The student who proofed the proclamation has become its historian.
choices.historicalContext: The press run that printed 1857's proclamations was the same industry that grew into the vernacular newspapers and print culture of the later nineteenth century — a direct line from war printing to public media.

ending.title: Letters Against the Siege
ending.text: You were educated for a century that did not yet exist, in a city that did not yet exist either — both were being invented while you studied. The rising closed the schoolrooms, but it never closed the book you were writing. What you carried out of 1857 was not a victory and not a defeat, but the grammar of a new era: a language in which the old city and the new empire could finally speak to one another — and argue.
lessons: Cities like Delhi raised literate networks of Persian, Urdu, Arabic and English learning in the decades before 1857.
Printing presses and proclamations made words a weapon in the war — studied by both sides.
Indian writers left their own records of the siege, which historians weigh against British accounts.
The education system rebuilt after 1858 carried the division between English and vernacular into the modern age.

title: The Court and the Two Flags
tagline: June 1857 — a princely court in central India
disclaimer: FICTIONAL RECONSTRUCTION. This scenario is created for educational purposes and is based on documented historical conditions. You are playing a fictional character — it does not represent the exact life of a specific historical individual.

intro.youAre: You are a ruler of a middling princely state in central India — a treaty ally of the East India Company whom the Company has yet to annex. Your court maintains the old forms: durbar, title, order. Beyond your border, garrisons are rising; the emperor's name is being used in proclamations calling on you to turn your arms against the Company.
intro.where: A princely state in central India
intro.context: Your position is precisely the one the Company fears and the proclamations court: a ruler with a treaty, an army of his own, and neighbours rising across the border. The Company that guaranteed your throne is the same Company that extinguished the thrones of Satara, Nagpur and Jhansi — under the doctrine the tribunal named 'lapse'.

narrative: Behind the durbar's silver doors, your real audience is a file. A treaty. An armed resident.
The proclamations speak of honour and faith; the Company speaks of subsidies and salt-posts.
Every envoy who enters your gate carries a flag you may have to follow or refuse to your cost.

stages.title: The Envoys
stages.description: Two parties arrive at your court in the same week. From the rebel side, a messenger reading the emperor's proclamation — a call to Hindus and Muslims 'to stand by one another' and rise against the Company, promising protection of religion and property. From the Company, the resident's aide: a crisp request for troops, money and routes, 'in accordance with the treaty of alliance.' Both wait in the forecourt for your word.

choices.label: Honour the treaty and send aid to the Company
choices.summary: Provide troops and money as the alliance requires.
choices.consequence: You send a contingent and a credit to the Company side. The resident thanks you with unusual warmth; neighbouring rulers hear of it. Through the months of the rising your state is left in peace, and after 1858 your treaty is renewed on terms better than most — but the price is sharp: your own durbar quarter is full of men who whisper that you served the foreigner against your own countrymen.
choices.historicalContext: The great majority of princely rulers stayed loyal to the Company in 1857, aided by the undertones of the conflict and by Company arms. Loyalty drew subsidies and security — and a crowd of critics among their own people.

choices.label: Weigh the proclamation and join the rising
choices.summary: Turn your troops toward the rebellion.
choices.consequence: You reason as your envoys urge: the Company has broken its own oaths at Satara and Jhansi, and this is the moment to strike. Your cavalry rides to join the columns. For a season you are celebrated in the proclamations as a defender of the faith and of the country. Then the reconquest reaches your border, your forts fall, and before the year turns, your durbar is a pension and your titles a memory.
choices.historicalContext: Most rulers who joined the rising lost their thrones; a few, like those of Bundelkhand's smaller lords, fought until the end. The proclamations' promises of protection were real only as long as the rebellion held ground.

choices.label: Delay and play for time
choices.summary: Keep both envoys waiting through the season.
choices.consequence: You stall with plausible courtesy — 'the state must consult its council' — while your ambassadors sound out both sides. The Company's resident grows cold; the rebel envoy grows loud. Everyone in your durbar talks of your 'wisdom'; everyone at your borders talks of your weakness. When the Company finally wins, as you half-knew it would, you are forgiven as one who 'wavered but did not fight.' Your throne survives, and so does your reputation for something men call perhapsness.
choices.historicalContext: Delaying, hedging and buying time was the classic strategy of the weaker ruler in 1857 — perilous but survivable. Historians note how many thrones were kept by rulers who committed nothing and enabled everything.

stages.title: The Border
stages.description: A rebel column crosses your border seeking refuge, and the Company demands you deny it — 'stand with the lawful government, prince.' But the column carries the emperor's name, and your own officer corps contains men who answer to that name. It is your court's hardest hour: half the state wants the column fed and quartered; the other half wants it turned away at the guns' point.

choices.label: Deny the column passage and hold the border
choices.summary: Order your troops to hold the frontier against the rebels.
choices.consequence: Your border posts fire a single volley of warning, and the column wheels away — the Company reports your 'firm adherence to the alliance.' Inside the state, desertion begins: a third of your army slips off to join the column against your orders. The loyalty of your own colours, after that volley, is never again what it was.
choices.historicalContext: The 'loyal' rulers who held their borders against rebel columns paid for it in the loyalty of their own troops — sepoys, retainers and cavalry answered older calls than treaties.

choices.label: Shelter the column, in secret if possible
choices.summary: Allow the men to rest in the forests of your marches.
choices.consequence: Your officers guide the column away from the roads and into the forests of your marches, where it stays two weeks. The Company's officers find nothing but trails. When the rising finally ends, the men who sheltered with you remember it to their grandchildren; the Company's intelligence remembers something too, thinner, and it weighs on your subsidies for a decade.
choices.historicalContext: Rulers and zamindars who quietly aided rebel columns while professing loyalty exploited exactly the ambiguity that most threatened the Company — and most protected their own houses when the war ended.

choices.label: Negotiate a neutral corridor
choices.summary: Buy the column's passage with food and safe conduct.
choices.consequence: You send an eminently practical proposal: the column will move around your state in exchange for supplies, and the Company will see your goodwill. Both sides accept; nobody is entirely fooled; there is a quiet poetry in your durbar that a ruler has 'bought his peace with supplies and a signature.' The ledger of alliances, so often written in blood, is written this season in grain.
choices.historicalContext: Supply and safe-conduct agreements were unofficial contracts of the war — rulers, zamindars and merchants all sold passage, and the archives preserve both the receipts and the denials.

stages.title: The Reward
stages.description: At last the storm passes. The reconquest is complete; tributary arrangements are being re-drawn across India, and your state is being assessed as a friend, a neutral, or a liability. An officer of the new Crown government presents himself: 'Her Majesty's government will remember the conduct of the state in the late disturbances.' Your durbar must decide what sort of reputation it means to inherit.

choices.label: Press for the rewards of loyal service
choices.summary: Claim the honours, titles and arrangements owed a faithful ally.
choices.consequence: You press your claim, and the Crown responds in the idiom of the new dispensation: your state is renewed, your titles confirmed, your embassies received at the new order's courts. It is the friendship of power, formal and durable. You have done what a treaty ruler does — survived, and been remembered for it, in the clean column of the ledger.
choices.historicalContext: After 1858 the Crown rewarded loyal princes with renewed treaties, adopted-heir recognition and honours. The loyalty of the princes became a pillar of the post-1857 settlement — the mirrors of the throne.

choices.label: Rebuild quietly and keep the durbar modest
choices.summary: Accept the quiet terms and rebuild the state's own strength.
choices.consequence: You take the modest settlement, keep your court small, and put the state's resources into canals, troops and granaries rather than ceremony. A generation later your state is one of the best-run in central India, and its ruler is a quiet fixture of the century's long peace. You have traded glory for competence — and been repaid many times over.
choices.historicalContext: The princely states that flourished after 1858 commonly did so through competent, non-heroic administration — the very antithesis of the durbars' pomp. Progress and prudence, not defiance, secured their futures.

choices.label: Hold a quiet court and record the truth
choices.summary: Keep your own chronicle of who did what — and why.
choices.consequence: You instruct a learned clerk to write the state's true account of the disturbances: who aided the Company, who sheltered the column, whose grain kept the roads open — an honest chronicle of survival kept under the throne. It is the account of a ruler to himself, and it is the one document no conqueror will ever own. When historians one day open the family's papers, they will read — under the honours — the true costs of the year.
choices.historicalContext: Royal and courtly chronicles of 1857 exist — kept under the honours of the new dispensation — and are among the valuable sources for the rulers' perspective. Some were read by nobody for a century.

ending.title: The Durbar After the Storm
ending.text: You walked the length of 1857 between two flags, and you are still seated beneath a throne. Whatever the chronicles now write about your wisdom, you know the arithmetic of the year: survival cost some of everything, friendship with power cost a little more, and honour — in the old sense — was a commodity that no treaty could price. The court endures. The country endures. Both are yours to account for.
lessons: Most princely rulers remained loyal to the Company; those who rose, mostly lost their thrones.
The doctrine of lapse — as at Satara and Jhansi — was a standing grievance among rulers who kept their oaths.
Border politics, supplies and safe-conduct could buy a throne even when an army could not.
The Crown's post-1857 settlement built its order on loyal princes as much as on armies.

title: The Crown of the Mountain
tagline: June 1674 — the eve of the coronation at Raigad
disclaimer: FICTIONAL RECONSTRUCTION. This scenario is created for educational purposes and is based on documented historical conditions. You are playing a fictional character — it does not represent the exact life of a specific historical individual. The meters below are a gameplay device, not a historical score.

intro.youAre: You are the master of Swarajya — a state built from hill forts, valley loyalties and oaths, now grown from the ghats to the coast. Your coronation as an independent sovereign is being prepared at the mountain capital of Raigad.
intro.context: For months the court has debated the ceremony: which rites, which lineage, which priests. The coronation will declare to the sultanates and the empire that the Maratha country is no client but a sovereign state. The rituals are as political as they are sacred.

narrative: A crown is a wall built of ceremony higher than any fort.
Every lord, priest, envoy and merchant watching these days will carry the story of them to a different court.
The mountain has been your witness since before the other kings knew your name.

stages.title: The Question of the Rites
stages.description: Learned Brahmins debate whether the consecration fitting a sovereign can be performed for your lineage, and which ceremonies must be observed. Some demand purifications that take months; others warn that delay breeds rumour. Outside, envoys from the Portuguese and English factories wait — and the empire watches for a sign of weakness.

choices.label: Undertake the prescribed purifications
choices.summary: Accept the long, costly preparatory rites demanded by the priests.
choices.consequence: The rites are performed with full solemnity, and the lineage question is settled by the scholars' verdict. The preparations cost treasure and months, and a few complain the state should spend on powder rather than prayer — but when the day comes, no court can call the coronation irregular.
choices.historicalContext: The historical coronation was indeed delayed by disputes over the Kshatriya rites and by preparation; priests and scholars were brought from varied centres, and the ceremonies that followed were elaborate and expensive.

choices.label: Send for the learned of every tradition
choices.summary: Assemble sufficient witnesses and scholars to make the consecration beyond dispute.
choices.consequence: Envoys ride out to bring learned and influential figures to Raigad. Some arrive, some send gifts and letters. The assembly is larger and more impressive than it would have been, and the chronicles count the great names present — but the delays try the patience of your captains, who want a king crowned yesterday.
choices.historicalContext: The Raigad coronation drew a great assembly — nobles, officials, and observers from the European factories and neighbouring states — which is part of why the event is so well attested.

choices.label: Crown quickly, rites as they can be done
choices.summary: Press for the ceremony within the season, omitting what can be trimmed.
choices.consequence: The coronation proceeds swiftly and the mountain holds its festival while the rains still held off. Some priests refuse parts of the ceremony; a faction whispers that the full rite was cut short. Your captains are pleased — but so is the empire's news-writer, who sends word that the ceremony was done in haste.
choices.historicalContext: Haste would have been a real temptation, but the historical coronation was performed with full elaboration — which itself signals how much weight was placed on legitimacy over speed.

stages.title: The Preparation of the Mountain
stages.description: Raigad receives its great day's dress: flags on the ramparts, the great drum tuned, waters fetched for the rites, gifts from all the provinces of Swarajya and beyond. The court must decide who stands nearest the throne, how the foreign factors are received, and what title the new era shall carry.

choices.label: Make the assembly as great as the realm allows
choices.summary: Spend rank and treasure on a spectacle every court will hear of.
choices.consequence: The assembled throng is vast — nobles from the forts, chiefs of the ghats, and the foreign factors in their best. The chroniclers count thousands. Your treasury is lighter and your reputation, as the news travels, is heavier than ever. One old captain mutters that a kingdom is not a fair, but he stands closest when the drum sounds.
choices.historicalContext: Contemporary accounts describe a large and richly dressed assembly on the mountain, with the companies' factors present — the scale of the event is one of the best-attested features of the coronation.

choices.label: Honour the captains of the ghats above the envoys
choices.summary: Give the fort-holders and the mavals the places of honour.
choices.consequence: The men who bled for the forts stand close to the throne; the foreign factors stand politely further back. One factor writes home of a slight; the captains write nothing — they simply remember. The coronation binds the war-band tighter than any treaty, and this, the old guard say, is the true crown.
choices.historicalContext: The authority built by the movement rested on the loyalty of its commanders and the hill people; the historical coronation honoured and consolidated that warrior nobility.

choices.label: Proclaim a new era in your own name
choices.summary: Start the count of years from the coronation, as sovereigns do.
choices.consequence: The courts of the Deccan begin, slowly, to date letters by a new era — some mocking, some hesitating. It is an audacious and modern gesture: time itself becomes the claim. When the era is abandoned after your death, the memory of that sovereign punctuation of history lingers in the records.
choices.historicalContext: The initiation of a new era (and of separate dating) at the 1674 coronation is associated with the assertion of independent rule, though its practical adoption was limited and short-lived.

stages.title: The Day of the Crown
stages.description: The rains have held their breath. The throne is set, the umbrellas raised, the priests intoning, the drum sounding over the valleys. As the gold is laid upon you — with the words that make you sovereign — you look out over the fort you built and the country that chose you, and you know the years to come belong to whoever holds this crown well.

choices.label: Accept the title of Chhatrapati
choices.summary: Take the imperial-style sovereign title before the assembly.
choices.consequence: The word carries through the Deccan: a sovereign has risen in the ghats, crowned beyond the reach of the sultanates and the empire. The title becomes a banner that rivals and successors will fight to carry for a century. You have turned a mountain stronghold into the seat of a dynasty's claim.
choices.historicalContext: The coronation and the Chhatrapati title were the movement's declaration of sovereign legitimacy — the claim the later Maratha state and its rivals inherited.

choices.label: Vow protection of faiths and of the land
choices.summary: Bind the new crown, publicly, to protect worship and cultivation alike.
choices.consequence: The vow is remembered long after the gold has been put away: a sovereign who swore on the crown to guard temples, mosques and fields of every community under his hand. When later rulers weigh tolerance against zeal, your words on the mountain remain a standing measure.
choices.historicalContext: Swarajya's administration cultivated legitimacy across communities; Shivaji's recorded policy of protecting places of worship and cultivators, and respecting the rites of other faiths even while asserting sovereignty, is documented in the period's evidence.

choices.label: Turn the mountain into festival
choices.summary: Give the people their share of the day — food, gifts and celebration.
choices.consequence: The gifts and the feasts set the fort alight with relief and joy; the ghats below see a mountain burning bright for a week. The memory of the day fixes the coronation in the people's hearts — and folk memory, you have learned, is a fort that no army storms.
choices.historicalContext: The coronation included distributions and festivities recorded in the chronicles; communal celebration was integral to its political effect.

ending.title: Sovereign of the Mountain
ending.text: The crown came to the mountain, and the mountain kept it. What you built was not only forts — it was a claim so firm that the sultanates and the empire could no longer pretend you were their servant. The coronation of 6 June 1674 told every court and country the same thing: here, in the Maratha country, a sovereign has risen. Whatever came after, that single day on the windswept fort made Swarajya a name that no power could unmake.
lessons: Legitimacy in the 17th-century Deccan was built with ceremony as much as with arms.
The coronation declared sovereignty against both the Deccan Sultanates and the Mughal empire.
The title Chhatrapati became a banner inherited by the whole Maratha state after 1674.
The assembly and foreign observers at Raigad make the coronation among the best-attested events of the reign.

title: The Decisive Meeting
disclaimer: FICTIONAL RECONSTRUCTION. This scenario is created for educational purposes and is based on documented historical conditions. You are playing a fictional character — it does not represent the exact life of a specific historical individual. The meters below are a gameplay device, not a historical score.

intro.youAre: You are a soldier of the maval country — a hillman of the ghats who has followed your leader since the fort-captures began. The armies of Bijapur, sent to crush everything you have built, are camped in the valleys below the new fort.
intro.where: Pratapgad and its passes, Satara hills
intro.context: Afzal Khan of Bijapur holds the plain with a large force. Your leader has met him to talk. No one knows what the meeting will bring; the passes must be watched, the fort held, and every moment of the encounter kept secret until it is done.

narrative: The hills have ears, and today every ear is trained on the same meeting.
A fort is only as strong as the men who watch its passes when the valley is full of the enemy.
If the meeting goes wrong, the whole country will hang on how fast the word travels — and on who holds the high ground.

stages.title: The Enemy in the Valley
stages.description: Below the fort the Bijapur army spreads across the fields — horsemen, musketeers and the baggage of a great campaign. Your captain orders the gates barred and the passes watched. As night falls, a messenger confirms the two leaders will meet at the foot of the hill tomorrow.

choices.label: Hold the walls and watch the valley
choices.summary: Keep every post armed and every eye on the enemy camp.
choices.consequence: You stand the night watch on the ramparts, counting campfires. When the morning comes and the meeting begins below, the fort is ready — powder dry, fuses lit, the gates braced. Whatever happens in the hollow, the high ground will answer for you.
choices.historicalContext: Forts and the high passes were the decisive advantage of the movement; holding them while giving battle in the valleys was the pattern of raiding and defensive warfare documented in the campaigns.

choices.label: Scout the meeting ground by night
choices.summary: Creep down to learn the lie of the ground where the leaders will meet.
choices.consequence: You thread the dark hills and come back with what you need: the hollow, the trees, the path the general must climb, the place where men could be hidden. When the order comes, your company moves like it belongs to that ground — because you have seen it with your own eyes.
choices.historicalContext: Intimate terrain knowledge of the maval soldiers was the military foundation of the movement, and reconnaissance of the passes preceded every action of the period.

choices.label: Prepare the men and hold them steady
choices.summary: Move among the company, still nerves and keep faith together.
choices.consequence: You pass the night by the cooking fires and the muster points, speaking plainly with the young soldiers who have never faced a host so large. When the meeting below ends in a shout, your line does not waver: each man steps up as though the ground were his own field.
choices.historicalContext: Cohesion of small, kin-like units was a hallmark of the movement's army, whose strength lay in reliable hillmen rather than in numbers of raw levies.

stages.title: The Meeting
stages.description: The word comes down like thunder: the meeting has turned. What exactly happened in the hollow — who struck first, what was said — will be argued for centuries. All you know is the signal, the shouting, and that Afzal Khan's camp has suddenly become a headless army. Now the order is given: fall on them from the fort and the passes before they can form.

choices.label: Fall on the camp with the fort's men
choices.summary: Strike the disordered host at once, from the heights.
choices.consequence: You come down with the colours, and the panic is all one way. The Bijapur force has no general, no order — only tents, treasure and road. By evening the passes are full of fugitives and your own men laden with what a great campaign had carried up the hills. Never again will a sultanate dismiss Swarajya as a band of hill robbers.
choices.historicalContext: The outcome of 10 November 1659 — the general's death and the rout of his army, with the high passes sealing the disaster — is attested across the sources; the precise events of the meeting itself remain debated.

choices.label: Seal the passes first, strike at the retreat
choices.summary: Deny the enemy every way out, then harvest the retreat.
choices.consequence: Your company takes the western defile just in time: the fugitives heading for the Konkan meet a wall of pikes in a fold of the hills. The retreat becomes a rout that carries nowhere safe. Some say you let treasure escape through a side path to save speed — but no one who sealed the pass at sunset doubts what you did.
choices.historicalContext: The narrow passes of the ghats made retreat as deadly as defeat for the Bijapur forces — the same terrain advantage the movement used again and again.

stages.title: The Mountain Keeps Its Name
