stages.description: Three days later, the valley is quiet. The prisoners are being ransomed or let go; the captured war-treasure is being counted; and the news is already riding on every road — to the Konkan ports, to Bijapur, to the empire. One general is dead, a host is gone, and a new power stands before the Deccan as what it always said it was: sovereign of its own country.

choices.label: Garrison the captured ground
choices.summary: Hold what the win has opened — the road to the Konkan.
choices.consequence: You are ordered forward with the first garrisons sent toward the coast, holding the captured passes and towns that the victory laid open. Swarajya gains its sea-facing provinces, and your name is written in the grants that parcel out the new country. The battle's fruit is land, and land is its own kind of loyalty.
choices.historicalContext: After Pratapgad the movement advanced toward the Konkan coast, gaining ports and revenues — the documented territorial result of the campaign.

choices.label: Carry the first news to the country
choices.summary: Be the man who brings the word of the victory home.
choices.consequence: You ride the ghats with the news, and the valleys throw open their doors to you — grain, water, blessings, and the questions of every chieftain who wants to know if it is truly over. You learn, riding that road, that news is a weapon the movement will keep using with as much care as any siege.
choices.historicalContext: News of the victory spread rapidly and shaped the movement's reputation across the Deccan; the reporting of events was itself a political act of the period.

choices.label: Bury the fallen and tend the wounded
choices.summary: See to the accounting of the dead, friend and foe.
choices.consequence: You spend the days after the fight with the surgeons and the priests, naming the dead, mending the wounded, and burying the strangers who died for a general they would not memorialise. A soldier remembers the victory in banners; you remember it in the quiet of the ground where friends and enemies lie equally. The country is safer, and it is also poorer — and you carry both truths with you.
choices.historicalContext: War's human cost — dead, wounded and displaced across the countryside — is part of the documented record of the campaigns, even where specific casualty numbers are not precisely known.

ending.title: The Pass Remembered
ending.text: You were one soldier among hundreds on a mountain that decided the fate of a country. The meeting in the hollow, the camp thrown into confusion, the passes sealed — the details would be argued over for centuries. What you know, from where you stood, is simpler: an army sent to erase your people from the hills was erased instead. After that day, when the drums of the Deccan spoke of the Maratha power, they spoke of an enemy that had become a nation.
lessons: Terrain and the high passes were the movement's decisive advantage.
The outcome of 10 November 1659 is documented; the events of the meeting itself are debated between sources.
The victory opened Swarajya's expansion toward the Konkan coast.
In a raiding, mobile army, shock and speed mattered more than numbers.

title: The Rain Falls, the Gate Opens
tagline: July 1660 — the besieged fort of Panhala
disclaimer: FICTIONAL RECONSTRUCTION. This scenario is created for educational purposes and is based on documented historical conditions. You are playing a fictional character — it does not represent the exact life of a specific historical individual. The meters below are a gameplay device, not a historical score.

intro.youAre: You are a soldier of the garrison inside the great fort of Panhala, blockaded for months by a Bijapur army under Siddi Jauhar. Food is running short, the monsoon has turned the world to water, and tonight your leader intends to slip through the enemy's lines.
intro.context: The blockade has tightened since March. Siddi Jauhar's camps ring the fort; every route out is watched. The escape that is being prepared will move not by force but by timing and terrain — and the foe must not learn of it until the party is gone.

narrative: The rain is the only friend that will move tonight.
A fort is a promise: as long as men hold the wall, the country below still has a name.
If the escape is to work, every step must be as quiet as the drop of rain on stone.

stages.title: The Hungry Walls
stages.description: Rations are down to a handful. Siddi Jauhar's lines circle the mountain, and a message has returned from the search for a way out: there is a route, but it passes close to the enemy watch-fires and crosses the worst ground of the ghats. The captains are told tonight may be the night.

choices.label: Silence the gate and muffle the party
choices.summary: Prepare a silent departure that the camp will not hear.
choices.consequence: The gate is oiled, the horses wrapped, every bell silenced. Word is passed man to man without a horn or a shout. When the wicket swings in the downpour, the enemy hears nothing but the rain — and the first the camp knows of the escape is the dust (or the mud) of the morning after.
choices.historicalContext: The documented escape of 13 July 1660 was conducted by night in heavy rain, using a little-known route — precisely the kind of terrain-dependent, secretly-arranged movement the hill forces excelled at.

choices.label: Light decoy fires to hold the enemy's eye
choices.summary: Send part of the garrison to draw the watch the other way.
choices.consequence: Feints at the eastern wall pull the enemy's watches and a couple of their pickets onto false ground. The main gate opens while they are looking the wrong way, and the escape party is away down the west face. The decoys slip back behind the walls before dawn — tired, breathing hard, and quietly proud.
choices.historicalContext: Deception, feints and diversions were standard tools of the hill warfare documented across the campaigns; a sleepless or misdirected enemy was worth a whole garrison of extra men.

choices.label: Move fast and trust the mountain legs
choices.summary: Abandon stealth for speed — outrun the camp's response.
choices.consequence: The party moves with the freedom of men bred in the ghats, eating distance in the dark. The pursuit is slower — harnesses catch, horses flounder, orders shout across the wet blackness. You gain the head start, but the risk was real: one stumble, one mis-sound, and the whole gamble would have collapsed into a running fight in the dark.
choices.historicalContext: The movement's soldiers were famed for mobility in the ghats; speed was a form of defence even against far larger forces, as documented in the campaigns of the 1660s.

stages.title: The Pursuit
stages.description: Day breaks grey and wet. The alarm has gone up behind you — tracks found, horns blown, a detachment of horsemen and infantry hurrying onto your trail. Ahead lies the long road to Vishalgad, and between you and it there is a defile where a small party could stop an army — or be caught and destroyed.

choices.label: Volunteer for the defile
choices.summary: Take a chosen few and hold the pass while the rest rides on.
choices.consequence: You serve the rearguard in the defile, and you learn what a handful of men can mean when the ground is theirs. The pursuit surges, breaks, and surges again, and each time the pass holds. By the time the leading rider of the party reaches Vishalgad, the defile has cost the pursuit its afternoon — and cost the rearguard its bravest. Several do not walk out; the memory of the pass keeps them for you.
choices.historicalContext: The action at Ghod Khind (Pavankhind) — a rearguard stand in a defile that covered the escape to Vishalgad, and in which Baji Prabhu and his brother fell — is the documented core of the flight, even as the chronicles colour the details.

choices.label: Split the party to confuse the chase
choices.summary: Send a false group one way to draw pursuit off the true road.
choices.consequence: Your group takes the false track, dragging folds of cloth through the mud and leaving every sign the hunters expect. The pursuit follows you for hours into a dead valley before the ruse is found — and by then the true party is far ahead. You rejoin at the rendezvous with your skin, and a new story to tell about the mud.
choices.historicalContext: Decoying and misleading pursuit was a practiced art in the Deccan's guerrilla warfare and is described in the period's accounts of fast-moving columns.

choices.label: Turn and check the pursuit at the ford
choices.summary: Hold the crossing long enough to break the chase's nerve.
choices.consequence: You make a stand at a rain-swollen ford, and the first horsemen who press into the water pay dear for it. The pursuit's captains call a halt to count their losses, and the halt stretches into delay. When the army finally crosses, the trail is hours cold — the march of a people's leader into the hills has become, in one stroke, a successful retreat.
choices.historicalContext: Delaying actions at natural bottlenecks — fords, defiles, passes — recur throughout the Raiding warfare of the period and were a core tactical necessity for smaller forces.

stages.title: Vishalgad and Beyond
stages.description: The fort of Vishalgad appears through the rain, and the escape is complete. Behind you, the pass tells its story in the silence of those who did not come through. The blockade of Panhala has produced, instead of a captured king, a legend of a night march and a mountain kept against an army. The country will feed on this for years.

choices.label: Stand the defence of the refuge
choices.summary: Hold Vishalgad and the surrounding hills until the siege is lifted.
choices.consequence: You take post on the walls of the refuge while the pursuit camps sullenly below. Provisions, powder and patience carry the weeks; a detachment sent from the rest of the country finally clears the approaches, and the siege of the escape dissolves. When you ride down at last, the country opens to you as to men who have come back from the dead.
choices.historicalContext: After reaching Vishalgad, the escape party and the relief directed by the movement secured the position; the 1660 campaign ended without the movement's leader being captured.

choices.label: Spread word of the escape to the country
choices.summary: Ride ahead so the valleys know their leader is alive.
choices.consequence: You carry the news across the valleys, and the effect is like water in a dry field: everywhere the people hear their leader slipped free of the great siege, hope returns with the rain. The story of the pass is told and retold until it passes into the memory of the whole country — becoming, in time, one of the founding tales of the Maratha spirit.
choices.historicalContext: The flight from Panhala became a celebrated tradition of the movement; the transmission of such stories was itself a documented feature of how the Maratha country remembered its founding era.

choices.label: Tend the fallen of the pass
choices.summary: Return to the defile to honour those who did not come through.
choices.consequence: You walk the pass again in the quiet weeks after, counting the marks of the fight and marking the ground where the rearguard's captains died. What you find — the torn cloth, the spent weapons, the silence — you carry home as a kind of scripture. In the years that follow, when they raise a shrine and a story at Pavankhind, you will be among the men who can testify: it was true, and it was as costly as they say.
choices.historicalContext: The memorialisation of Pavankhind — in tradition, story and later inscription — is itself part of the historical record of how the flight was remembered.

ending.title: The Defile That Saved a Nation
ending.text: Every account of the flight from Panhala agrees on the shape of it: a leader who gambled his life on a night march, and a rearguard who gave theirs in a defile so that the rest could live. The rain, the mud, the pass — these were not scenery. They were the difference between a captured king and a legend. You walked out of that July with the mud of the ghats on you, and with the knowledge that some walls are not made of stone.
lessons: The night escape of 13 July 1660 (traditional date) turned near-defeat into survival.
The rearguard stand at Ghod Khind — Pavankhind — cost the lives of Baji Prabhu and his brother.
Terrain knowledge and deception were the movement's greatest weapons against larger armies.
The story of the flight became one of the founding memories of the Maratha country.

title: The Fort Above the Field
tagline: c. 1646 — a valley below Torna Fort
disclaimer: FICTIONAL RECONSTRUCTION. This scenario is created for educational purposes and is based on documented historical conditions. You are playing a fictional character — it does not represent the exact life of a specific historical individual. The meters below are a gameplay device, not a historical score.

intro.youAre: You are a cultivator in the valley beneath Torna Fort. For a generation your fields have paid revenue to the officers of the sultanate's commandants, and the fort above you has changed governors without ever changing your life. Now word spreads that a young lord of the neighbourhood is taking the high places — and that he promises to govern better than those who came before.
intro.where: A valley below Torna Fort, Pune hills
intro.context: The fort of Torna has fallen into the hands of Shivaji — by persuasion and surprise, the accounts say. The change of lordship on the hill above may change the demands on your field below: who will collect, at what rate, and whether the new men are better or worse for the village.

narrative: The fort looks down on the valley, and tor the valley the fort has always been the tax-gatherer's weather.
A new master on the hill is like a new monsoon: everyone hopes, nobody knows.
The clever farmer listens more than anyone and commits less than anyone.

stages.title: A New Flag on the Summit
stages.description: The banner on Torna changes, and the commandant's deputy rides down to take the tallies of the villages. There is talk that the new lord will leave fields alone and tax only trade; there is also talk that he needs grain for a fort full of men. Either way, the harvest is coming, and the collector is on the road.

choices.label: Wait, listen, and keep your grain in the field
choices.summary: Hold off committing until the new collector's terms are known.
choices.consequence: You keep the harvest standing a day longer than prudence allows and send your sons to the well-side and the market to see who arrive. Whenthe collector's deputy comes, you know already what he will ask — and you negotiate, village by village, from the strength of having seen him coming. The new lord's first revenue round is gentler than the old one's last.
choices.historicalContext: Villages learned to read a change of lordship through its first revenue demands; the terms and rates of collection were the practical face of any new power for the countryside.

choices.label: Pledge grain to the new fort
choices.summary: Offer supplies openly, and ask for protection from raiders.
choices.consequence: You deliver grain through the summer, marked in the new registers, and receive a written promise of protection. When a band of raiders descends from the ghats, officers sent from the fort do answer — the promise is honoured. The village pays, but it also sleeps; and next season, when the old sultanate sends a collector to test the new lord, your name is in the book of those the fort protects.
choices.historicalContext: The early movement's legitimacy rested on the promise of better and fairer government; protection for villages was the concrete form that promise took, even where its consistency should not be overstated.

choices.label: Hide a share of the harvest in the hills
choices.summary: Bank a surplus against whichever master turns out worse.
choices.consequence: You stash grain in a cave your grandfather marked, against the day when a bad year follows a changing ruler. The village survives the next requisition with a skimpy look to it — and the stored grain feeds the household in the late summer when others scrape. The hiding costs you a little honour and a few lies, and buys you the rarest thing in the valley: a margin.
choices.historicalContext: Hoarding and concealment of grain were standard village defences against requisition in the war-torn Deccan of the 1600s, documented across the region's revenue history.

stages.title: The Campaign Season
stages.description: The new power rides out on its first campaigns, and the valleys around you fill first with its own men and then — after word of the fights — with fugitives and rumour. Soldiers march past the fields; your best pair of bullocks is eyed twice. Every village must decide how much to offer, how much to hide, and how to stay alive between armies.

choices.label: Furnish carts and forage to the new army
choices.summary: Support the camp locally and accept its papers.
choices.consequence: Your carts and grass feed the column through the season, and the officers write you a chit against future revenue — honoured, to everyone's surprise, at the next settlement. The burden is real but regular, and the village learns that under this flag, an army takes what it needs WITH a receipt. Some call it heavy; you call it legible.
choices.historicalContext: Armies requisitioned carts, fodder and grain; the movement's administration is associated with more orderly revenue and written obligations, though records of actual practice are uneven.

choices.label: Move the precious stock off the road
choices.summary: Drive the best cattle to kin in a side valley until the march passes.
choices.consequence: The cattle spend the season with a cousin in a fold of the hills, out of the column's way, and your fields are worked by hand and patience. When the army moves on, the stock returns — fat, in its way, and alive. The technique of 'reading the road' keeps the household intact while the country moves past it.
choices.historicalContext: Moving livestock and moving households to kin was a documented strategy of farming communities during the campaigns that crossed the Deccan.

choices.label: Refuse the requisition and hide the carts
choices.summary: Pretend you have nothing, and hope the column passes.
choices.consequence: The ruse holds for a day, and then a search turns the barn's loosened axle into proof of the lie. The carts go anyway — with a fortnight's fury added to the taking. Nothing is killed, but the grain store is thinner and the officers' memory of this valley is warm. In a year of war, refusing has a price; you pay it, and you remember it.
choices.historicalContext: Villages that refused requisitions drew searches and confiscations; the balance between hospitality, concealment and refusal was the practical politics of every valley.

stages.title: The Year After
stages.description: By the following season, the new power has held the hill through a full round of sowing and harvest, and the revenue registers show a steadier hand than the sultanate's commandants ever offered. The fort above the field is now a settled part of the skyline — and every village in the valley is asking the same question: has this lordship earned its place over the field, or is it only the old wolf in a new flag?

choices.label: Put down seed and trust the new order
choices.summary: Plant for a settled future under the new master.
choices.consequence: You sow your best fields early, borrow seed, and bet on the new order's regularity. The rains come, the harvest is real, and the new collectors keep their promised rates. By the end of the season the fort above the field is no longer a stranger's roof but, in its way, your own government's — and the valley's confidence in it spreads with the seed.
choices.historicalContext: The movement's early success depended on convincing the countryside that its rule was better — more regular, less rapacious — which the documented revenue experiments partially delivered.

choices.label: Keep a foot in both worlds
choices.summary: Pledge lightly to the fort and quietly to the old order's contacts.
choices.consequence: You pay the new collectors their due and keep quiet letters open toward the old sultanate's networks. It costs you a little honour and a few meetings in barns, and it buys the household insurance against whichever tide turns. For a farmer, survival is not a banner; it is a crop in the barn and a son alive. This is the wisdom of the valley, and you live it.
choices.historicalContext: Villagers and village headmen commonly kept relations with more than one authority while it was possible; such multiple loyalties are documented in the revenue histories of contested Deccan territories.

choices.label: Petition the fort for a written rate
choices.summary: Ask the new rulers to fix the village's demand in writing.
choices.consequence: You walk up the mountain and stand in line before the fort's office, and — to the astonishment of every elder — a written paper comes back naming the village's fixed dues. It is not a promise of paradise; it is a promise of predictability, and in the Deccan of the 1600s predictability was worth more than gold. The paper becomes the village's talisman and the seed of its loyalty.
choices.historicalContext: Written settlement of revenue demands — making the state legible and bounded — was among the most valued innovations associated with the rising Maratha administration.

ending.title: The Fort Becomes a Roof
ending.text: For the cultivator, the change of lordship on the hill was not a battle but a weather system: it altered the rain of demands, the timing of the collector, the safety of the harvest. The young lord who took Torna and promised steadier government was, for once, as good as a written line. A power that asks only what it has named, and protects what it has promised, earns the seed of the valley — and the valley, sowing, sows loyalty with the wheat.
lessons: For the countryside, a change of ruler meant a change of revenue — the practical face of every lordship.
The early movement traded on the promise of fairer, more regular government.
Villages used concealment, kin networks and written obligations to survive contested rule.
Documented revenue practice is the ground on which the movement's legitimacy was really built.

title: The Port with No Walls
tagline: January 1664 — the great port of Surat
disclaimer: FICTIONAL RECONSTRUCTION. This scenario is created for educational purposes and is based on documented historical conditions. You are playing a fictional character — it does not represent the exact life of a specific historical individual. The meters below are a gameplay device, not a historical score.

intro.youAre: You are a merchant with a shop and a warehouse in Surat — the richest port of the Indian Ocean's western side. Your goods, your credit and your family's future sit in the lanes around you. And this January, word is racing down the road that a Maratha army out of the Deccan is marching on the town.
intro.where: Surat, the Mughal emporium on the Gujarat coast
intro.context: Surat has no proper walls. Its wealth is defended by the sea, by the Mughal name, and by the assumption that no one would dare. The Deccan's new power, three hundred miles of bad road away, has just disproved the assumption. Traders, factors and shroffs all speak of flight; the town's protections are about to be tested.

narrative: Credit is a rumour, and rumour is now the only credit that works.
A port's true walls are the confidence of its merchants — and confidence has just taken the road south.
Somewhere between the demand to save the goods and the need to save the family, every merchant in Surat must choose.

stages.title: The Word on the Road
stages.description: The first riders reach the gate with alarmed faces: an army has crossed the passes, moving swiftly, taking supplies and not pausing. The town's notables meet in the coffee-house lanes; some merchants have already packed wives and ledgers toward the ships. The question is before every trader's door — quick passage to safety, or stay and guard the stock?

choices.label: Stay and guard the stock
choices.summary: Remain with the warehouse and see which way the storm turns.
choices.consequence: You stay, and in the days that follow you are among the handful who can still move goods when the raid hits — and among the handful who are required to. Your warehouse loses a heavy share, but your standing suffers nothing, for the town remembers who remained while others fled. In the reckoning after the raid, presence becomes reputation.
choices.historicalContext: The raid of January 1664 fell on a largely unwalled town; merchants' accounts, English factory letters and Persian chronicles all record the sack and its costs.

choices.label: Shift your best goods to the hire-boats
choices.summary: Move the movables out on the river while there is still time.
choices.consequence: Under last light you transfer your finest bales and your ledgers onto boats bound upriver. The raid finds your warehouse half-empty, and your family's core capital survives — at the price of weeks in the reeds and a season of your trade's goodwill where you laded goods without permission. Survival is a kind of solvency, but it does not always pay interest.
choices.historicalContext: Moving goods onto boats and toward the hinterland was a documented merchant response to raiding on the coast; the monsoon rivers and creeks were used as escape routes.

choices.label: Cultivate the fort's and the factory's men
choices.summary: Build relations with whoever might protect — or ransom — your goods.
choices.consequence: You spend the days before the raid close to the English factory and the qazi's circle, making yourself known, useful and remembered. When the town falls, the factory's compound holds a set of people whose names matter later — and your name is among them. You lose goods; you gain a network that outlasts the year's losses.
choices.historicalContext: European factory compounds and prominent local households were the focus of attempts at protection during the sack, as the English records themselves show.

stages.title: The Taking of the Town
stages.description: The army is in the lanes. Shops are broken, warehouses emptied, the great houses stripped, and even the European factors' chests are being carried off. In the chaos, every merchant must decide how to meet the raiders: hide further, negotiate, or move among the soldiery and buy back what can be bought.

choices.label: Hide the silver in the false floor
choices.summary: Conceal the last bullion where no search will reach.
choices.consequence: The false floor under the storeroom holds through the searches that turn over the house twice. When the army leaves, you are one of the thinner but solider merchants of the port — and the first to re-open a reliable line of credit in a town where everyone else's word is in ashes. Hidden silver becomes visible standing.
choices.historicalContext: Merchants concealed bullion and records below floors and in walls during the sack; the survivors' capacity to re-issue credit was crucial to Surat's recovery.

choices.label: Redeem goods directly from the soldiers
choices.summary: Move among the raiders and buy your own stock back.
choices.consequence: You pass among the soldiery buying back your own bales at a fifth of their true worth — a bitter arithmetic, and a hazardous one, for the soldiers respect no precedent of ownership. You recover a slice of your goods for a fraction, and the loss is survivable. It is also, you learn, how the town will be rebuilt: bit by bit, from ruin-bought returns.
choices.historicalContext: After sacks and raids, merchants commonly bought back plundered goods from the soldiery — a practice recorded in the literature of Indian Ocean ports under attack.

choices.label: Plead for the town's protection with the raiders' officers
choices.summary: Use your standing to bargain for an exemption for certain houses.
choices.consequence: You face the officers' captains with gifts and eloquence, and secure a mark on a few compounds — your own and your kin's — that spares them the worst. The town learns the mark is as good as a wall. From the ashes you emerge as a broker between worlds: the man who could talk to the new power. In the years that follow, that is worth more than the lost bales.
choices.historicalContext: The raid was followed by negotiations, ransoms and the payment of protection arrangements; mediators who could speak to the Deccan power became valuable figures in Surat's politics.

stages.title: After the Fire
stages.description: The army has gone, back over the passes with its treasure. Surat is poorer, smokier, and humbler; the Mughal governor is sending dispatches all the way to the court, and the European factors are demanding indemnities that will be argued over for a decade. The town must rebuild its credit, its quays and its belief in itself. Merchants who survive the winter will define what the port becomes.

choices.label: Re-open early and lend to the rebuild
choices.summary: Bet on the port's recovery by resuming credit at once.
choices.consequence: You are among the first to unboard and to honour old debts while your own are still being counted. The gesture is remembered; within a season your name heads the lists of the town's sound men, and the flow of trade, like water, reoccupies the channel you kept open. Leaders in the market, as on the land, are the ones who re-sow first.
choices.historicalContext: Surat recovered its trade remarkably quickly after 1664 in historical terms; the early resumption of credit by surviving merchants was the mechanism of that recovery.

choices.label: Invest in the town's future walls
choices.summary: Press the notables to build the protection the port never had.
choices.consequence: You put your name and your purse behind the building of fortifications and the stationing of a garrison, in coalition with the factors who suffered the same loss. The walls rise slowly, in the arguments of committees, and eventually the port has a strength to match its pride. The next raid, years later, finds Surat a harder target — and your children inherit a better defended name.
choices.historicalContext: After 1664 the question of Surat's defences became a live political issue, and the town's vulnerability was a standing theme in the English factory's complaints.

choices.label: Diversify the routes — the sea and the Deccan
choices.summary: Open trade toward the new power's ports instead of only the Mughal road.
choices.consequence: You begin, cautiously, to send factors toward the Konkan outlets that Swarajya's coast now commands — diversifying your routes so that no single lord can take everything you are. Some call it trading with the raiders; you call it reading the map as it is. In time the new ports grow into legitimate harbours, and you are standing where the old and the new roads meet.
choices.historicalContext: The growth of the Konkan ports after the movement reached the coast created new commercial opportunities that traders and pilots gradually exploited.

ending.title: The Ledger of the Raid
ending.text: January 1664 burned up a great deal of Surat's wealth and pride, and the merchants who weathered it wrote the port's next chapter. The raid announced a new power to the Indian Ocean — and it taught every trader on that coast a hard lesson about walls, credit and the difference between knowing where wealth lies and being able to hold it. In the aftermath, the survivor's craft was the same as always: measure the loss, re-sow the trust, and read the map as it is, not as you wish it were.
lessons: The sack of Surat in January 1664 is documented in English factory letters and Persian chronicles.
Un-walled wealth was hostage to any power able to reach it.
The raid put Swarajya on the map of Indian Ocean politics.
Credit and trust were the true walls of the port — and the first to be rebuilt.

title: The Building of the Mountain
disclaimer: FICTIONAL RECONSTRUCTION. This scenario is created for educational purposes and is based on documented historical conditions. You are playing a fictional character — it does not represent the exact life of a specific historical individual. The meters below are a gameplay device, not a historical score.

intro.youAre: You are a master builder — a mason and carpenter of the hill country, skilled in stone, timber and the watercraft of tanks and channels. A new sovereign-in-the-making has taken the great plateau-fort of Rajgad and wants it rebuilt as a capital: gates, reservoirs, palaces, workshops. Your craft is now a matter of state.
intro.context: The fort's plateau must be transformed: great gates fitted, cisterns and tanks dug and lined, dwellings and storehouses raised, and the crown walls made worthy of a kingdom that is still being invented. For a builder, this is a generation's work, and it begins with a summons.

narrative: Every fort the enemy surrenders, a craftsman must build.
Stone is patient; rulers are not.
The water that fills a tank on a mountain summit is saved by the hands that line its bed.

stages.title: The Summons
stages.description: Word reaches your town that the new lord of the hills wants masters — masons, smiths, timber-men — at Rajgad, and will pay in grain and coin, with exemption of dues for the season's work. Half the trade calls it a trap; half calls it the chance of a generation. The mountain is a long walk with all your tools.

choices.label: Go up with your tools
choices.summary: Answer the summons and drive a fair bargain.
choices.consequence: You climb to Rajgad and stand on the plateau, and the work is as real as promised: gates to be set, cisterns to be bound, workshops to be framed. You bargain hard — grain now, coin when the gate opens — and the officers keep their word. Your name enters the fort's roll of builders, and the wall you raise will carry your hand's mark.
choices.historicalContext: The fortifications attributed to Shivaji's reign required large construction work — skilled and unskilled labour drawn from the surrounding areas — which is documented in the material record of forts like Rajgad.

choices.label: Send apprentices first, gauge the terms
choices.summary: Commit your young men, and join once the terms prove good.
choices.consequence: Your apprentices climb first and return with honest reports: the pay is regular, the officers are straight, and the work is worthy. You follow, a season late and with a pocket of questions answered. The fortress gains your craft at full strength, and you gain a position of the work without ever having to petition for it.
choices.historicalContext: Craft labour moved between patrons by reputation; the speed with which a fort of Rajgad's scale was built implies a substantial pool of skilled regional labour responding to the new patron.

choices.label: Stay and keep your town's craft
choices.summary: Work locally, and serve the mountain with goods instead of hands.
choices.consequence: You stay below and supply lime, timber and worked iron to the fort's buyers. Your craft feeds the summit without climbing it, and the village Trade continues while the mountain rises. When the fort's officers press for skilled hands, your name is on the list of reliable suppliers — a credit that turns to your household's protection in hard years.
choices.historicalContext: Forts drew on surrounding villages for materials and support; supply contracts and requisition alike connected the new power to the craft economy of its neighbourhoods.

stages.title: The Work of the Plateau
stages.description: The mountain is a world under construction: stone hauled by ropes and winches, lime burned in great pits, timber dragged up the escarpment, and the water of the rainy season to be caught before it escapes over the edge. The schedule is the monsoon's — once the rains begin, walls must be up and cisterns lined.

choices.label: Bind the waterworks before the walls
choices.summary: Dig and line the tanks and cisterns so the fort can live and siege.
choices.consequence: You throw your craft into the tanks, and when the monsoon comes the summit drinks — storage that in a siege is worth a thousand matchlocks. The officers understand, and your mastery of water is spoken of at the daily muster. A fort that can hold its own rain can hold its own freedom.
choices.historicalContext: Water-harvesting tanks and cisterns on forts like Rajgad are among the most significant surviving engineering works of the period; their construction reflects deliberate planning for defence.

choices.label: Set the gate workings and the crown walls
choices.summary: Give the fort its doors and first defence.
choices.consequence: The great gates take form under your hands — the strapping, the pivots, the masonry jambs, the killing-holes above. The day the first gate swings true in its socket, a cheer goes up from the labour gangs. Workmen say the gate is the fort's face, and you have given this face honour before the enemy ever comes to knock.
choices.historicalContext: The gateways and bastions of the period's forts are among their most distinctive surviving features, showing careful stone masonry and defensive planning.

choices.label: Build the workshops and the stores
choices.summary: Raise the spaces where armour, powder, grain and craft will live.
choices.consequence: You frame the workshops and storehouses that allow the fort to work as a town: smiths under cover, grain in dry lofts, powder away from fire, and iron and timber accounted. When the sovereign arrives for a long stay, everything he needs already has a room named for it — and the officers begin to call the plateau 'the master's city'.
choices.historicalContext: Forts of the period functioned as administrative and storage centres with workshops, granaries and treasuries; the developed Rajgad fits this documented pattern.

stages.title: The Fort That Holds
stages.description: Season follows season, and the summit becomes a capital. One morning you stand on the crown wall and look down over the valleys you walked up from — fields, roads and distant forts — and understand that the work of your hands has outlived the need for it to be merely useful. The mountain keeps the country. In the years ahead, your students will build other forts in its image.

choices.label: Teach the next generation of builders
choices.summary: Pass the loot of a lifetime of craft to younger hands.
choices.consequence: You take sons of the craft under your eye — the level, the plumb, the discipline of the lime and the line — and when the state needs more forts raised, there are two dozen hands who can raise them properly. The craft becomes part of the country's strength, carried by people who will never hold a sword but will hold every wall that the sword protects.
choices.historicalContext: The building tradition of the Maratha forts was a regional inheritance passed between generations of craftsmen; its masterwork is still visible in the forts' standing ruins.

choices.label: Turn your hand to the armourer's work
choices.summary: Shrink your craft into the weapons the walls will need.
choices.consequence: You learn the armourer's arts at the fort — straps, buckles, matchlock fittings, the repair of harness — and the summit's defence deepens with your forge. The price is the fine stonework you used to love. But in the years of campaign, when the fort must arm and re-arm, the officers count you with the soldiers, for your craft has become a weapon.
choices.historicalContext: Forts maintained armourers and workshops for weapons and their repair; the craft production of fort-basing armies is documented in the records of the period's strongholds.

choices.label: Take the summit's earnings home to the valley
choices.summary: Return with your due, and build the prosperity your neighbours share.
choices.consequence: When the term of your service is met, you go down with grain, coin and letters of exemption, and the valley gains a house rebuilt, a debt cleared, and a reputation for having sent up a master who came back whole. Other craftsmen follow your road up the mountain; the loop between the valley's skill and the summit's need grows, and the country stitlaker together by that thread.
choices.historicalContext: Craft and labour moved seasonally between valleys and fort-works in the period; the rewards of fort service flowed back into housing, tools and village economies.

ending.title: The Stone That Became a Kingdom
ending.text: You were a builder, not a banner, and you did what every fort in the country depends on: you made the mountain hold. The tanks you lined, the gates you hung, the workshops you framed — they turned a stronghold into a capital, and a capital into the seat of a state. When the chronicles speak of Rajgad, they will speak of the sovereign who commanded it. But the stones know better. The country was also built by hands like yours, and it remembered.
lessons: The construction works attributed to Shivaji's reign turned forts like Rajgad into functioning capitals.
Water-harvesting systems were among the most important engineering achievements of the forts.
Forts functioned as towns — workshops, granaries and treasuries as well as walls.
The 'history from below' of the Maratha state includes the un-named craftsmen who built it.

title: The Child in the Fort
tagline: 1630 — the town of Junnar below Shivneri
disclaimer: FICTIONAL RECONSTRUCTION. This scenario is created for educational purposes and is based on documented historical conditions. You are playing a fictional character — it does not represent the exact life of a specific historical individual. The meters below are a gameplay device, not a historical score.

intro.youAre: You are a householder of Junnar, the old town that lies in the shadow of Shivneri Fort. Your life is water, grain, market and festival — and the knowledge that the fort above you can change masters without changing your work. This winter, the fort's Maratha family is awaiting a child, and the town is full of excitement, prophecy and fear.
intro.context: The 1620s have been hard years in the region — famine and disease have touched the country, and the Deccan is full of the troubles of competing lords. The birth of a son to the fort's family is, for most people, a small and distant matter. For the family itself, and for the seers and servants of the fort, it will come to mean a great deal.

narrative: A town is a thing that watches: it notices who allows the markets, who keeps the roads, and who bears what name in the fort above.
No one in the market knows that the child born in the fort will be counted, later, by the whole country.
For now, the child is simply news — a lucky hour to name a festival, a reason for grain to be given.

stages.title: The Town in a Hard Winter
stages.description: The season is lean. The wells hold, but the grain is dear, and there is talk of sickness in the villages up the valley. At the same time the fort is alive with preparation — a birth is expected, and the town has been told the family will distribute grain in thanks. Some are for climbing to the gate for the dole; others for staying away from the crowds and the sickness.

choices.label: Take the fort's grain at the gate
choices.summary: Accept the distribution and be counted in its papers.
choices.consequence: You stand in the queue at the gate and receive your dole of grain, and your name is written in the distribution roll — a small document of an obscure kind, but one that binds the town to the fort's family in gratitude. In a hard winter the dole is bread; the roll is a kind of allegiance, signed in the waiting line.
choices.historicalContext: Fort families and lords distributed grain on occasions of festival and rite in the 17th-century Deccan; such distributions anchored local loyalty and were recorded in period documents.

choices.label: Keep the household close and the stores hidden
choices.summary: Avoid the crowds; guard what little you have.
choices.consequence: You stay within your own walls through the lean season, bartering quietly and avoiding both the queue and the cough. The household comes through the winter intact though thin. When spring arrives you are among the neighbours with a full boxcupboard left — and among those who must explain, at every festival, why they did not go up to the fort for the dole.
choices.historicalContext: Famine and epidemic years hit the Deccan in the late 1620s; households that could isolate and conserve survived better, a documented pattern of village response to dearth.

choices.label: Carry a small gift to the fort's servants
choices.summary: Offer your goodwill in the old way — a little curd, a cloth, a blessing.
choices.consequence: You climb with the neighbours and offer modest gifts to the fort's people at the time of the birth, as custom holds neighbours to do. The servants remember you among the well-wishers, and in the years to come — when the fort becomes more famous and its family looks back at the days of the child — the town holds a faint claim on its goodwill that costs you nothing and warms the memory of the town.
choices.historicalContext: Customary gifts and expressions of goodwill between town and fort households are recorded in the social practices of the Deccan; they formed one of the bonds of neighbourhood loyalty.

stages.title: The Name in the Fort
stages.description: The child is born — a son — and the fort rings with music and the distribution of grain and sweets to the gathering town. The seers announce the name, and the gate is opened wide for the celebration. For the town this is a few days of relief in a lean year; for you it is also a moment to decide how you will remember this house of the fort in the years ahead.

choices.label: Join the feast and the blessings
choices.summary: Take your place in the celebration, and carry its story home.
choices.consequence: You eat your share of the festival and carry the news to the market then next day: a son, born at the fort, given the name of a deity and blessed by the town's elders. In the retelling, the town begins to keep this child's story — the first of many tellings, for the child, as the country will learn, is carried by the people's memory as much as by any army.
choices.historicalContext: Birth traditions of the period involved distribution, naming rites and local celebration; the memory-tradition of Shivaji's birth became a fixture of Maratha collective identity long before the historical records were written.

choices.label: Note the omens with the elders
choices.summary: Sit with those who read meanings into the child's arrival.
choices.consequence: You sit late with the old ones who trade omens — a fort born in a famine year, a name from the god of auspiciousness, a gate thrown open in a lean season. The elders murmur that such a birth in such a house is not an ordinary thing. You carry that murmur for the rest of your life, and in the far future, when the child's name is on every lip, you will say simply: 'I was there when he was born under the sign of a hard year.'
choices.historicalContext: Auspicious and inauspicious signs attended birth in the period's social world; such traditions shaped how communities remembered events before formal records existed.

stages.title: The Long County
stages.description: Years pass. The child grows, and stories of the young lord of the ghats begin to reach even the market of Junnar: fort taken, companions sworn, valleys brought under one name. Your own household plants, harvests and pays what it owes — sometimes to one master, sometimes to another. And then, one market day, the town of Junnar must decide what it believes about the story that grew from the infant in the fort above.

choices.label: Tell the town what you remember
choices.summary: Testify to his beginnings when the new fame reaches the district.
choices.consequence: You become one of the old voices who can say, of the now-famous master of the ghats, 'I saw the fort gates opened for his birth; I stood in the dole-line of his infant dole.' The town listens; memory, you discover, is a kind of property, passed from the old to the young like a well-tended field. You have done your small part to make a man into a memory.
choices.historicalContext: Attestation of birth and early years in local memory contributed later to the written chronicles; oral tradition was a documented vehicle for the founding narratives of the Maratha state.

choices.label: Keep your distance from the great name
choices.summary: Live quietly; serve the crops, not the banners.
choices.consequence: You watch the new fame roll past your door like weather, and keep your household to its own road — sowing, hiding, paying a little to whoever can tax, and saying little in the market about the fort. It is not disloyalty; it is the caution of a man who has seen many banners. In the end your barn and your sons survive the century's changes, which is the market's quiet answer to every empire.
choices.historicalContext: Most commoners took no public part in the movement's rise; their lives of cultivation, commerce and caution were both the unwitnessed ground and the enduring base of the period.

choices.label: Give the memory a place in the town
choices.summary: Turn the seasons of the town itself toward remembering the child.
choices.consequence: Where you and the elders keep the story, a small place of memory takes root — a shrine or a festival day that ties the town's calendar to the fort's founding hour. It is a modest act of kinship between a town and a legend. In the centuries that follow, people will climb to places of that kind to touch the story with their own hands — and the town that first remembered will be remembered because it remembered.
choices.historicalContext: Sites of popular memory connected to Shivaji's birth and youth multiplied in the Maratha country, showing how a community's remembrance built the larger tradition.

ending.title: The Story the Town Kept
ending.text: You were nobody in the fort's history — a face in the queue, a name on a dole-roll, a neighbour at the gate. And you were everything, because the child who was born there entered the world in the arms of people like you, and the story of him was first sing in the market and the lane, not in the court. The country that came after was built of grain and stone and loyalty — and the loyalty, in the beginning, was simply this: a town that remembered the day the gates opened, and the child, and the promise of a hard year that somehow kept itself.
lessons: Local memory and town tradition were the first records of the movement's beginnings.
The birth date of 1630 is traditional; the later history is better documented.
Ordinary people were the witnesses, not the writes, of the founding decades.
The stories of a people are a kind of fort no army takes.

title: The Mountain Before the Crowd
tagline: June 1674 — the roads to Raigad and the day itself
disclaimer: FICTIONAL RECONSTRUCTION. This scenario is created for educational purposes and is based on documented historical conditions. You are playing a fictional character — it does not represent the exact life of a specific historical individual. The meters below are a gameplay device, not a historical score.

intro.youAre: You are a common person of the Deccan country that Swarajya has made its own. Word has passed through every town and village that the master of the mountain is to be crowned a sovereign at Raigad — and that the people are welcome on the roads, in the assembly, and at the festival of the day.
intro.where: The roads of the ghats and the platform of Raigad
intro.context: For a generation the country has known war, revenue and rumour. Now its ruler will be crowned in full public ceremony. For most people the coronation is less a matter of state than of spectacle and hope: a rare day when the people are told that a throne has at last been set in their own country, by their own hands-forged authority.

narrative: When a throne is set on a mountain, the people climb to see it.
The road to the crown passes through the villages, and the villages line it.
A country, too, must be crowned — and it is crowned by being present.

stages.title: The Road to Raigad
stages.description: Every road to the mountain is loud with movement: villages sending their notables with gifts and flowers, families walking for days to stand at the foot of a single ceremony. There is also cost — the journey takes time from the fields, and the way is crowded. The choice is plain: go up and be part of the day, or stay and hold the harvest.

choices.label: Walk up for the day
choices.summary: Join the pilgrimage of the ordinary people to the summit.
choices.consequence: You walk the ghat roads with your neighbours, singing and resting by the streams, and the climb itself becomes part of the event — a whole country climbing to see its own throne set. When you stand at the foot of the assembly, the miles are in your legs and the day in your memory, and you understand that a coronation is also a census: everyone who came is counted in the country's self-knowledge.
choices.historicalContext: Contemporary accounts describe a great assembly at the coronation, including a large crowd of the local people and notables; the movement's legitimacy drew visibly from the presence of the country itself.

choices.label: Send a gift and stay with the fields
choices.summary: Share in the day through a village offering, without the climb.
choices.consequence: Your village sends its bundle of good wishes — cloth, grain, flowers — carried up in the name of the neighbourhood, and you stay behind with the sowing and the calves. When the village's messengers return with the news and the small cloths handed back as keepsakes, the whole neighbourhood hears the day through their telling. Presence by proxy, but presence nonetheless.
choices.historicalContext: Village participation by offering and representation was a standard way rural communities took part in distant state ceremonies, documented across the period's gift-economy politics.

stages.title: The Day on the Mountain
stages.description: The platform is full: nobles in their finery, officers in armour, priests chanting, drums and trumpets, and around it all the pressed-back crowd of the people, silent in a way that itself sounds like awe. The gold umbrella is raised over the throne. The crown is laid on. A name, a title, a new calendar is declared — and the mountain roars.

choices.label: Let the roar out — and carry it home
choices.summary: Take part with your voice in the moment of the proclamation.
choices.consequence: Your shout joins the roar that rolls down the mountain and the people carry it through the valleys for weeks. When you return home, you become the town's witness of the day — tillers and weavers alike gathering to hear how the gold came down on the mount, and how the country before you stood and honoured its own. The memory of the sound becomes the memory of the state.
choices.historicalContext: The proclamation of the Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674 was accompanied by ceremony and celebration attested in the accounts; the aural and festive memory of the day carried forward into tradition.

choices.label: Watch quietly and remember for yourself
choices.summary: Hold your own counsel on a day of noise.
choices.consequence: You stand near the edge of the crowd and watch the ceremony with your own eyes, saying little.Weeks later, asked what it was like, you will be able to describe it with the precision of a witness rather than the colour of a caller: the gold, the crowd, the breath of the mountain held and released. Some hold the day by shouting; you hold it by keeping it. Both are ways of carrying a country's crown.
choices.historicalContext: The number of ordinary witnesses is unknown, but the documented assembly and the later interest of the country suggest a genuinely public and remembered ceremony.

stages.title: The Country After the Crown
stages.description: The festival is over; the rains come; the fields are planted again. The crowning changes no single furrow, yet something has changed in how the country speaks of itself: the fortress-state now has a crowned head, and its courts, roads and names are being made anew in that light. For you and the neighbourhood, the question is quiet and practical: what will the king's peace and the king's tax mean for the coming years?

choices.label: Plant for the king's peace
choices.summary: Bet the season on the promise of ordered rule.
choices.consequence: You sow your fields under the new sovereign's peace, and the collector comes when he says, at the rates he said, and the harvest stands its ground. The regularity of it is the miracle: a country that gives its word and keeps it. In the years that follow, when trouble comes from outside, you will find that the taxed and the protected have grown a single conviction — better one honest king of your own than many strange masters.
choices.historicalContext: The movement's revenue administration aimed at regularity and constraint; the practical experience of the countryside under the new state's rule shaped the loyalty documented in the period records.

choices.label: Mend what the wars broke
choices.summary: Use the peace to restore the household's line.
choices.consequence: You spend the settled seasons repairing what a generation of campaigns wore down: the tank, the cart, the barn, the family's standing in the village. Peace, you find, is a working material like stone or timber — you can build with it only if you use it while it lasts. By the end of the decade your holding is sounder than it has been in a lifetime, and the crowning of the mountain has, in its quiet way, bought back the furrow.
choices.historicalContext: After decades of campaigns and contested rule, the consolidation of Swarajya brought a period in which the countryside could rebuild — a documented outcome even where village specifics are not individually recorded.

choices.label: Keep a plain record of the day for the young
choices.summary: Leave the memory as a letter, simple and honest, for the next generation.
choices.consequence: You mark down the day in your own hand or your own telling — the climb, the gold, the roar — so the children of the village know that their country was crowned before their faces. When the written histories and the chronicles come later, they will not be built from nothing: behind every 'great' account stands an ordinary witness who kept the story simple and true. That is your politics, and you bequeath it.
choices.historicalContext: Popular memory and the later chronicles of the coronation draw on the lived tradition of the people who were present; the documentation of the event rests partly on such transmitted memory.

ending.title: The Crown the Country Carried
ending.text: The mountain held the ceremony; the country held the meaning. To the nobles it was legitimacy, to the envoys a fact to report to distant courts, and to the empire a challenge. But to the man and the woman in the crowd, it was simpler and stranger: their own country's master, crowned before their eyes, on a fort their own hands and fathers' hands had helped to raise. The crown came down to the mountain, and the crowd took it home in their voices and their memory — so that when the rulers changed and the empire came and went, the people kept the sure knowledge that a throne had once been set in their own country, and that they had been there to see it.
lessons: The coronation of 6 June 1674 was a public, attested event with a large assembly.
The event asserted sovereignty against the sultanates and the Mughal empire.
Popular memory of the day outlived the ceremony and fed the later chronicles.
For ordinary people, the crown mattered as a promise of regular peace.
